title: Show HN: Modelpeers – a changelog for the AI models and agents you use
author: liorgrossman
body: Earlier this year, I had one of my product's features down for 48 hours because Anthropic retired Claude 3 Haiku. In another instance, an API parameter started returning errors.I grew sick of not being able to follow and track the endless changes of AI models every week, so I decided to build Modelpeers. It's basically a feed of all these changes. You can follow models and agents that you use to see what is changing and what you need to do about it. Optionally, you can sign up to get a digest for the models/agents you follow.Every few hours, it downloads and hashes dozens of pages from the prominent AI companies' pages, like changelogs, deprecation pages, status pages, and pricing pages. Then when a page changes, it pulls the diff, validates it with two models, and if validated as true, it posts it to the feed.The feed currently has about 400 changes, 21 of them breaking changes.Fun fact (well, not really fun): OpenAI alone has 12 shutdowns/cutoff planned for the next six months.Would love to hear what y'all think.

### What trending means

A topic is trending when more Reddit authors used its words that month than usual. Activity is compared with recent months and, when available, the same month a year earlier, so regular seasonal spikes do not count. Related words that rose together are grouped into one topic and ranked by how unusual the change was.

Trends and their titles are generated automatically from public Reddit activity and headlines, without human review. A title can be imprecise or misleading. Trends reflect how much people discussed something, not whether it is important, accurate or endorsed.

title: Show HN: Uncracked City, detective game where you question LLM suspects that lie
author: passkey1510
body: To give you some context on the project. I'm a solo founder and I use AI heavily in my work. The idea came from wanting players to discover cities. Each city has its own history, so every case is set in a real city with real public places. The crime and the people are on other hand invented. The part that I care most is the playable aspect of the game, a model plays the detective and must solve the case before it goes live.As of today: it's free on Android, the iOS version is still waiting to be reviewed by Apple. It's available in six popular languages, but adding more languages is just a matter of time and demand.My long term vision if it takes off: weekly cases, private parties like a team-building escape game, an MCP so a game master can build their own scenario from ChatGPT or Claude, and maybe tourism offices since players travel the world.

## Topics

## Top Contributors

- tc-mb (213 contributions)
- davide-troiani (30 contributions)
- Halcao (26 contributions)
- oreomaker (20 contributions)
- hNSBQZ (6 contributions)
- dongfengwuyishi (4 contributions)
- MurphyWang (2 contributions)
- QWQ-potato (2 contributions)
- chmod777john (2 contributions)
- ZMXJJ (1 contributions)

---

## README

# MoEShift

**Large AI models on your Mac. Starting with 10 GB of RAM.**

**125 billion parameters. Up to 11 tokens per second. Under 10 GB of
peak process memory.** MoEShift is optimized for Apple Silicon: on a Mac mini
M4 Pro with 24 GB of unified memory, it runs Qwen 3.8 Flash Next with roughly
half the peak process memory of Strata and processes long prompts 2.6× faster.

MoEShift leaves room for your other apps, helping your Mac stay responsive during inference
instead of grinding to a halt under memory pressure. Keep browsing, writing
and coding while the model works—all locally, with no cloud subscription.

Qwen 3.8 Flash Next running locally with MoEShift in OpenCode

*Qwen 3.8 Flash Next running locally with MoEShift, connected to OpenCode.*

**Alpha release.** The core runtime is working, and the project is evolving
quickly. You may encounter rough edges; your feedback helps shape the next release.
Tested models and quantizations are listed below.

## Tested models and benchmarks

| Model | GGUF architecture | Tested quantization |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 Flash Next (125B) | `qwen4exp` | ISTA-DASLab GSQ-RCO IQ3_XXS |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | `qwen35moe` | UD Q6_K XL (Q6_K/Q8_0 experts) |

Both use the shared SSD expert runtime on Apple Silicon. See
supported architectures.

### Qwen 3.8 Flash Next

Compared with **Strata**, a popular choice for local MoE inference, on a
**Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB unified memory**. Both ran Qwen 3.8 Flash Next
(125B), ISTA-DASLab GSQ-RCO IQ3_XXS, with an 8,192-token context, no cached prompt
tokens and 256 output tokens. Strata: 0.2.7, build 0.1.52.

Inference time, peak process memory and prompt processing: MoEShift versus Strata

| Measurement | Short prompt: MoEShift / Strata | Long prompt: MoEShift / Strata |
|---|---|---|
| Input tokens | 66 / 66 | 6,009 / 6,009 |
| Inference time ↓ | **29.6 / 42.1 s** | **63.3 / 129.9 s** |
| Prompt processing ↑ | — | **160.8 / 61.8 tok/s** |
| Text generation ↑ | **10.44 / 8.4 tok/s** | **9.9 / 7.8 tok/s** |
| Peak process memory ↓ | **6.4 / 14 GB** | **7.5 / 14 GB** |

Time includes server-measured prompt processing and generation, excluding
startup. Memory is macOS `footprint -p` peak physical process footprint.

### Qwen3.6-35B-A3B

UD Q6_K XL on the same Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB unified memory.
Medians of three measured runs after warmup, with no cached prompt tokens and
512 output tokens, using the benchmark runner.
These runs use different output lengths from the Flash Next comparison above.

| Measurement | Short prompt | Long prompt |
|---|---|---|
| Input tokens | 72 | 6,060 |
| Inference time ↓ | **34.25 s** | **49.45 s** |
| Prompt processing ↑ | - | **417.24 tok/s** |
| Text generation ↑ | **16.50 tok/s** | **14.66 tok/s** |
| Peak process memory ↓ | **5.4 GB** | **5.6 GB** |

## What you need

- A **Mac with Apple Silicon** (M-series).
- At least **10 GB of RAM**.
- A fast SSD with space for both the GGUF and prepared expert files: at least
 **120 GB** for the Flash Next setup below, or about **60 GB** for Qwen3.6 UD Q6_K XL.
- Homebrew, the package manager for macOS. If you have never
 used it, follow its installation instructions, then return here.

## 1. Install MoEShift

Open **Terminal** and run:

```sh
brew install davide-troiani/moeshift/moeshift
```

The installation includes model preparation tools. MoEShift creates
`~/.config/moeshift/config.json` automatically on first launch and preserves
your settings on subsequent launches and upgrades.

## 2. Download the model

Choose a model and quantization from its download page:

| Model | Download |
|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 Flash Next | ISTA-DASLab GGUF files |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | Unsloth GGUF files |

Quantization is your choice: smaller files reduce storage and expert-cache memory;
higher precision requires more space and memory. The benchmarks above apply only
to the tested quantizations listed above.

Download all shards of your chosen quantization into the same folder, keeping
their names. Both models use the same preparation steps and the same
`~/.config/moeshift/config.json`; each has its own entry under `models`.

The commands below use Flash Next **GSQ-RCO IQ3_XXS** as an example:

- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-IQ3_XXS-00001-of-00002.gguf
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-IQ3_XXS-00002-of-00002.gguf

These two files total about **76 GB**. Reuse them if already downloaded.
MoEShift does not distribute or requantize models.

## 3. Get the downloaded model ready to use

Run this once to copy the model's specialized parts (“experts”) into files
MoEShift can read directly from SSD. Keep all original GGUF files.
Set `MODEL` to your GGUF (the first shard for split files) and `EXPERTS` to a
separate output folder for that model and quantization:

```sh
MODEL="$HOME/Downloads/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-IQ3_XXS-00001-of-00002.gguf"
EXPERTS="$HOME/Models/moeshift/qwen-iq3-experts"
MOESHIFT_PREFIX="$(brew --prefix moeshift)"
"$MOESHIFT_PREFIX/libexec/bin/python" \
  "$MOESHIFT_PREFIX/share/moeshift/tools/moe/experts.py" \
  extract --model "$MODEL" --out-dir "$EXPERTS"
```

Then check that the new files match the downloaded model:

```sh
"$MOESHIFT_PREFIX/libexec/bin/python" \
  "$MOESHIFT_PREFIX/share/moeshift/tools/moe/experts.py" \
  verify --model "$MODEL" --experts "$EXPERTS"
```

Wait for both commands to finish successfully. Verification compares the copied
weights with the originals. Keep the output folder intact (about **43 GB** for
the Flash Next IQ3_XXS example).
If interrupted, retry into a new empty folder and verify again.

## 4. Set the model paths in the configuration file

Run `moeshift` once to create the configuration, then stop it with Ctrl-C.
Open the configuration:

```sh
open -e "$HOME/.config/moeshift/config.json"
```

Inside `models` → your chosen model ID → `args`, replace these two values:

| Setting | What to enter |
|---|---|
| `model` | The full path to the **first** downloaded `.gguf` file. |
| `moe-experts` | The full path to the folder created in step 3. |

Use full paths in JSON (not `~` or `$HOME`), keep the quotes and commas, and save.
Both model profiles are included in the template. Existing user configurations
are preserved; copy the desired profile from the template
if it is missing. Use its model ID in API requests and clients. Leave the other
settings at their defaults for your first run.

## 5. Start MoEShift

```sh
moeshift
```

Leave this Terminal open. MoEShift starts a local server at
`http://127.0.0.1:8080`. Stop it with **Ctrl-C**. Next time, just run the same
command; you do not need to repeat the model preparation.

### Try a message from Terminal

Open another Terminal and run:

```sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"qwen-3.8-flash-next-rco-gsq-iq3-xxs","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello in one sentence."}],"chat_template_kwargs":{"enable_thinking":false},"max_tokens":128,"stream":false}'
```

### Connect your chat or coding application

In any client that supports an OpenAI-compatible API, enter:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Base URL | `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1` |
| Model | `qwen-3.8-flash-next-rco-gsq-iq3-xxs` |

MoEShift handles one inference request at a time and listens only on localhost.

## Architecture

Read the MoEShift architecture for the project’s design:
LES (Lookahead Expert Scheduling), expert loading and Metal execution, cache
policy, memory management, and server/worker lifetimes.

## Adjust speed and memory use

You can adjust these settings in the configuration file to suit your Mac.
With more RAM, you can increase `moe-prefill-bank` and
`LLAMA_MOE_PROTECTED_SLOTS` to keep more model data in memory and reduce SSD
reads. Lower them to use less RAM. For better control, change one setting at a time and restart
MoEShift to apply it.

| Setting | Default | Direct effect |
|---|---|---|
| `args.ctx-size` | `65536` | Maximum conversation length in tokens. Lower it to limit memory growth during long conversations; raise it to allow longer conversations, with more memory use as they grow. |
| `args.moe-prefill-bank` | `512` / `256`¹ | Expert cache used when reading your prompt. More slots can reduce SSD reads and speed up prompt processing, using more RAM; fewer slots save RAM. |
| `args.prefill-max-tokens` | `3072` | Amount of prompt text processed per batch. Smaller batches reduce peak working memory; larger batches can improve prompt-processing speed. |
| `env.LLAMA_MOE_PROTECTED_SLOTS` | `24` | Extra experts kept in memory while generating replies. More slots can reduce SSD reads and improve speed, using more RAM; fewer slots save RAM. |
| `args.threads` | `10` | CPU threads available to inference. More threads can help CPU work but compete with other apps; more is not always faster. |
| `env.LLAMA_GPU_KEEPALIVE` | `1` | Keeps the GPU active to reduce wake-up delays. Set to `0` to reduce idle GPU activity and power use, but expect lower speeds. |
| `env.LLAMA_MOE_QUIET` | `1` | Keeps expert diagnostics out of Terminal. Set to `0` for more detail when investigating a problem. |
| `port` | `8080` | Change this if another application already uses the port; use the same port in your client. |

¹ Flash Next / Qwen3.6. Slot sizes depend on the model and quantization;
equal slot counts do not imply equal memory use. The Flash Next defaults were
tuned on a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB unified memory. The
full configuration reference covers the remaining options,
valid combinations and command-line overrides. Settings under `env` are edited
in this file, rather than exported in Terminal.

## Feedback and issues

Found a problem or have an idea?
Open an issue,
after checking whether someone has already reported it.

Choose **Bug report** for installation, startup or inference problems, or
**Feature request** for suggestions, or **Benchmark result** to share measurements
from your Mac. The form guides you through the useful
information: your Mac chip and RAM, macOS version, MoEShift version, model files,
steps to reproduce and relevant Terminal output. Remove private prompts,
credentials and personal paths before posting.

## Contributing

See CONTRIBUTING.md for fixes, suggestions and pull requests.

### Share how MoEShift runs on your Mac

**Help someone with a Mac like yours decide whether MoEShift fits their day.**
Can you keep browsing in Safari while it answers? How does it feel on battery,
or with your usual apps open? Share a benchmark from your MacBook, Mac mini or
Mac Studio—every chip and memory size adds a useful piece of the picture.

You do not need a perfectly idle machine. Keep your normal setup and tell us
what you were doing. The benchmark runner handles the
fixed short and long prompts, repeats the measurements and creates a JSON report
for you. It collects benchmark metrics only; you describe your Mac and working
conditions yourself.

Then share your results
and attach the report. Screenshots and a few words about how responsive your
other apps felt are welcome too. Your experience can help the next user find

title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
author: ayanb9440
body: Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms. Kairos addresses two of the biggest problems facing traditional decisioning tools: a lack of labeled data to train on and dealing with fraudsters that are constantly changing their tactics.1. Traditional fraud solutions use ML models such as XGBoost to detect fraud, but these models are dependent on quality labeled data which many businesses do not have. We address this by using “System One” decision models in additional to traditional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. This allows you to incorporate plain language questions such as “Is this a throwaway email” into your decisioning, bypassing the need for large amounts of labeled data. This also allows you to capture aspects of fraud that are more unstructured, which is something that XGBoost models struggle with.2. Fraud teams are facing off with live players that are constantly changing their behavior to bypass the detection logic they have in place. You can train a detection model or define a ruleset once, but it will become obsolete in a matter of weeks as fraudsters figure out what your detection logic is. This means that you need a team regularly training models and updating rules based on new fraud patterns. Typically this takes a large data science/ML team. Kairos addresses this by introducing an MCP server, so that your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) can define a decision workflow, train models on your data, and pick the variant that performs best.You can self-host Kairos with Docker or use the hosted version at https://kairos.finic.ai

title: Show HN: A browser studio with a SPICE-modeled Juno 106 (playing Nightcall)
author: tonioab
body: I wanted the feeling of sitting down with a small "DAWless" hardware setup: a synth, some drums, a midi recorder, and knobs to turn. Something you can open for a quick jam, with enough care put into the sound that you’ll want to keep playing. The spirit is close to a DAWless setup, with the convenience of a browser tab.The linked demo is a recreation of Kavinsky’s Nightcall. It opens as a playable session, so you can listen, explore the instruments, and change the sounds yourself. All the audio is generated locally in your browser.I spent 80% of the dev time on Cybelle, a clone of the Juno-106, with a C++/WebAssembly sound engine. It was built with a SPICE model (model of the original circuit), which I then calibrated against my real hardware Juno. Reproducing the filter and the chorus took many iterations and blind tests, and I believe it strikes a good balance of audio fidelity and CPU performance for most laptops. To my ears, the Juno presets and filter sweeps sound the same between my hardware and Cybelle (as in, I can't differentiate them in blind tests).An interesting side-effect of using "hill-climbing" agentic loops to optimize the sound engine is that I ended up spending hours on the UI as well, trying to make it immersive and photo-realistic.I’d especially love feedback from people who make music with hardware: how does it sound, how does it feel to play, and what would make you reach for it when you have a few minutes to make music?

If you want direct browser-to-API calls (BYOK) or local Ollama models, edit the connect-src directive in source/src/app.html and rebuild grai.html with python3 scripts/build.py (included in the kit).
Do I need technical skills or coding? 
 No. In the default Copy-Paste mode, you open grai.html in your browser and paste your posts. You extract your Voice DNA and write. If you can use a browser and a text field, you can use grai.
What devices and systems does it run on? 
Runs natively on macOS and Windows as well as Linux in any modern browser. No installer or admin permissions needed. Tablets load the application and run the profiler, while the full three-column Writing Desk is optimized specifically for laptop or desktop displays. Phones are for reading, never for serious writing.
Where do my texts go, and can they be used to train AI models? 
The local grai.html app has no grai application backend and zero telemetry. Voice profiles and writing samples (along with drafts) are stored in your browser's localStorage when available. If your browser settings or private-browsing mode block localStorage on local file:// pages, grai falls back to in-memory session storage ( memStorage ), which lasts until the tab closes. Use the 1-click .grai backup export to save your profiles permanently to disk. Data leaves your machine in three cases: (1) when you paste and submit a prompt into Claude or ChatGPT (or Gemini) in Copy-Paste mode, or (2) when a custom BYOK build calls your selected API provider. It also leaves (3) when you voluntarily export and share a .grai file or PDF Dossier (such as over Slack or email, which sends the exported profile to that external communication service), or if your own browser syncs local data across devices.
How is it different from Custom Instructions in ChatGPT or Claude? 
Custom Instructions are a paragraph of preferences the model may ignore. grai measures your actual sentence lengths, openings and rhythm, stores that as a profile, and runs a deterministic 6-rule audit and CV ≥ 0.32 burstiness check over every draft in your browser. It highlights matching spans and offers targeted span repair while you keep final control over editing and copying.
What happens if my style changes in time? 
Re-run the profiler on recent posts. Compare the new metrics against your archived baseline with one click. Voice evolves, so grai adapts with your thinking instead of freezing past habits.
Can I make a backup if I change laptops or clear browser data? 
Yes. Click Backup Profiles to export all voice settings into a single local file. Restore Backup loads the file onto any new machine instantly. No cloud login required. When sharing with colleagues, remember that Restore replaces existing profiles on that device. Export your working set first.
How does the 30-day guarantee work? 
Buy it, use it for 30 days. If your writing is not visibly sharper and faster to produce, email [email protected] with your order number. Full refund, no forms, no questions.
Your unfair advantage
Build a personal brand voice nobody can imitate.
Take last week's post. grai returns a quantitative score and reveals the hidden structural patterns flattening your reach. You already suspected something was off. Focused local calibration removes the robotic tells before you publish.
Publish again in your real cadence. Not polite. Distinct.

What's in it
Everything you'd reach for Docker Desktop for.
Containers were the start. Kiri now builds and scans images, runs Kubernetes and whole Linux machines, and puts any container on the internet with one click.
Containers and Compose
Every docker command you use, Compose projects grouped in the window, and a page for each container with live logs, a shell and its files.
Images from Docker Hub
Search Docker Hub from the window and watch each layer pull. amd64 images run through Rosetta.
Builds, with a scan
docker build through BuildKit, a Builds view of every build, and a vulnerability scan of each image on its own page.
Kubernetes
kiri k8s start gives you a k3s cluster in about 20 seconds, with Pods and Services in the window. kind runs too.
Linux machines
kiri machine create dev --distro ubuntu : your user, sudo, and your Mac folders at the same paths.
Share
A public link for any container on runkiri.cloud , from the window or kiri share web . More .
Names and HTTPS
Apps open at web.kiri.local , Compose services at api.myapp.kiri.local , with HTTPS from Kiri's own narrow certificate authority.
Light on your Mac
Unused memory goes back while it runs, and the VM sleeps after a minute idle. The daemon stays around 15 MB; waking takes 0.15 s.
Move over in one go
Bring your images, volumes and containers from OrbStack or Docker Desktop, then switch docker to Kiri from the window.
Prefer the terminal?
The commands you already type.
With Kiri open, the ordinary docker command runs on Kiri, and kiri adds what Docker doesn't have: a name for every container, Kubernetes, Linux machines and a public link.
kiri run , kiri ps work like their docker twins.
web.kiri.localhost reaches a container by name, no port to remember.
kiri k8s start and kiri machine create for a cluster or a Linux box.
kiri share web puts it on the internet.
~ zsh 
$ kiri run --rm alpine echo "kiri" prints kiri.
 $ kiri run -d --name web nginx prints a container ID.
 $ kiri ps lists the running web container.
 $ curl http://web.kiri.localhost reaches it by name, with no port to remember.
 $ docker ps shows the same container, because Kiri answers the Docker API.
 $ kiri share web gives it a public link at web.runkiri.cloud.
Illustrative session. With Kiri open, the ordinary docker command runs on Kiri. 
Kiri Share
Send anyone a link to a container.
Press Share on a running container and it answers at a public address on runkiri.cloud , over HTTPS, until you press Disconnect. Show a client the branch you're on, test a webhook, or open your app on your phone.
Keep your name. Reserve myapp.runkiri.cloud and it's yours next time too.
Every computer, one list. Shares from your other Macs and PCs show up too, coloured by the machine they run on.
Visitors are warned. The first visit to a share shows a Kiri warning page before it opens, so a link can't pass itself off as your bank. View the warning page →

Getting started
From download to a public link in four steps.
Step 1
Install
Open the disk image and drag Kiri to Applications . It sets up docker for you.
Download for Mac 
Step 2
Pull an image
Search Docker Hub in Images and press Pull, or:
docker pull nginx 
Step 3
Run a container
Press Run and give it a port. It starts in milliseconds.
docker run -p 80:80 nginx 
Step 4
Share
Press Share on the container for a public link, or:
kiri share 80 
Compare
Same command, three routes.
OrbStack and Docker Desktop pass every container start through five programs, each with its own socket. Kiri passes it through one daemon that calls the kernel itself. Same docker command on all three.
docker run --rm alpine true 
10× slower 
 Real time 
Run again 
OrbStack Measured 0 ms 
Five hops. One shim process stays resident for every running container.
Docker Desktop Measured 0 ms 
The same five hops, and a shim per running container.
Kiri Measured 0 ms 
One daemon creates namespaces, cgroups and mounts itself. Nothing per container is left running. Most of this time is the docker CLI starting up. Through the Docker API, a whole container lifecycle takes 3.1 ms.
Medians from one full run on one Apple Silicon Mac, every engine limited to 2 CPUs and 8 GB, all three through the same docker CLI with Docker's default bridge networking. Stops are drawn evenly; only the totals are figures. Windows has its own race .
Full benchmarks: p99s, the Docker API path and every raw figure → 
How it works
One small VM. One daemon. A socket between them.
On macOS, Kiri boots a single Linux VM through Apple's Virtualization.framework, with a custom kernel and a small Rust init as PID 1. The host and guest talk over vsock. Inside, the Kiri daemon creates each container with clone3 . On Linux the same daemon runs on your own kernel with no VM at all, and on Windows it runs inside WSL2.
One VM, one daemon See the numbers → 
Boot once
 One VM serves every container. Cold boot to ready takes 112 ms , down from 810 ms on a stock kernel.
Talk directly
 Requests cross one vsock channel into the VM, not a chain of Unix sockets. A round trip takes guest vsock round trip p50">31 µs .
Leave nothing behind
 No process stays per container. OrbStack keeps a shim for each one: 143 running containers held 1.13 GB in shims on our test Mac.
Measured on one Apple Silicon Mac. Method and raw numbers are on the benchmarks page .
The app
A native app, not a web wrapper.
AppKit and the system WebKit on the Mac, Win32 and WebView2 on Windows, so no Electron and no bundled browser. Manage containers, images, volumes, networks and Compose projects, with live stats, logs, a terminal and files for each container. Running apps open by name at myapp.kiri.local . On the Mac it brings your images and volumes over from OrbStack or Docker Desktop, and lives in the menu bar.

What is Conecto?
The business tools your AI agent works in: 581 tools across 52 areas, like a CRM, an inbox, a phone line, invoices and books, all paid from one balance.

title: Show HN: Mallard: Git for the age of AI agents
author: rika321
body:
We started Mallard to make it easier to share our agent sessions and build things together.
We spend much of our working day talking to Claude and Codex. Those conversations include the ideas, designs, and decisions behind our work. However they often stay on one machine, without backups or an easy way to share them.3 months. 10 accounts on 20× plans. 100 billion tokens later, Mallard finally hatched.Share and back up agent sessions using Cloudflare R2, Dropbox, or Mallard Cloud.Explore the discussions and design decisions behind PRs, including Mallard’s hatching logs.Pull and resume sessions in Codex or Claude Code with the original context.For teams, Anthropic internally uses cloud VMs and Claude Tag so that teammates can work in shared agent conversations and pick up where others left off. Mallard lets teams achieve the same goal at almost zero cost, without any cloud VMs.We want Mallard to be free and easy to use for everyone, rich or poor.We built a lightweight version of GIT and reworked our storage protocol, removing CAS so Mallard can work with any cloud storage that supports LIST and PUT APIs. Bring your own storage or use Mallard Cloud. No Git server or expensive sandbox required.We also added one-click sign-in for Dropbox and Cloudflare R2, so anyone can connect their own cloud storage to Mallard in just a few clicks.We don’t think the internet, recommendation algorithms, or AI should be in the hands of just a few people. We hope Mallard helps more people share their work, find an audience, and have their voices heard.Free and MIT licensed. Available on macOS and Windows.
Website: https://mallard-ai.com/
GitHub: https://github.com/Git4Agent/mallard-app

# Traccia

Production-ready distributed tracing for AI agents and LLM applications

Traccia is a lightweight, high-performance Python SDK for observability and tracing of AI agents, LLM applications, and complex distributed systems. Built on OpenTelemetry standards with specialized instrumentation for AI workloads.

Traccia is available on PyPI.

## ✨ Features

- 🔍 Automatic Instrumentation: Auto-patch OpenAI, Anthropic, requests, and HTTP libraries
- 🤖 Framework Integrations: Support for LangChain, CrewAI, and OpenAI Agents SDK
- 📊 LLM-Aware Tracing: Track tokens, costs, prompts, and completions automatically
- 📈 OpenTelemetry Metrics: Emit OTEL-compliant metrics for accurate cost/token tracking (independent of sampling)
- ⚡ Zero-Config Start: Simple `init()` call with automatic config discovery
- 🎯 Decorator-Based: Trace any function with `@observe` decorator
- 🔧 Multiple Exporters: OTLP (compatible with Grafana Tempo, Jaeger, Zipkin), Console, or File
- 🛡️ Production-Ready: Rate limiting, error handling, config validation, robust flushing
- 🛡️ Guardrail Detection: Passive, zero-overhead detection of guardrails in traces — explicit, provider-native, and heuristic
- 📝 Type-Safe: Full Pydantic validation for configuration
- 🚀 High Performance: Efficient batching, async support, minimal overhead
- 🔐 Secure: No secrets in logs, configurable data truncation

### Installation

```
pip install traccia
```

### Basic Usage

```
from traccia import init, observe

# Initialize (auto-loads from traccia.toml if present)
init()

# Trace any function
@observe()
def my_function(x, y):
    return x + y

# That's it! Traces are automatically created and exported
result = my_function(2, 3)
```

### With LLM Calls

```
from traccia import init, observe
from openai import OpenAI

init()  # Auto-patches OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

@observe(as_type="llm")
def generate_text(prompt: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

# Automatically tracks: model, tokens, cost, prompt, completion, latency
text = generate_text("Write a haiku about Python")
```

### LangChain

Create a callback handler and pass it to `config={"callbacks": [traccia_handler]}`. Install the optional extra: `pip install traccia[langchain]`.

```
from traccia import init
from traccia.integrations.langchain import CallbackHandler  # or TracciaCallbackHandler
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

init()

# Create Traccia handler (no args)
traccia_handler = CallbackHandler()

# Use with any LangChain runnable
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")
result = llm.invoke(
    "Tell me a joke",
    config={"callbacks": [traccia_handler]}
)
```

Spans for LLM/chat model runs are created automatically with the same attributes as direct OpenAI instrumentation (model, prompt, usage, cost).

Note: `pip install traccia[langchain]` installs traccia plus `langchain-core`; you need this extra to use the callback handler. If you already have `langchain-core` (e.g. from `langchain` or `langchain-openai`), base `pip install traccia` may be enough at runtime, but `traccia[langchain]` is the supported way to get a compatible dependency.

### OpenAI Agents SDK

Traccia automatically detects and instruments the OpenAI Agents SDK when installed. No extra code needed:

```
from traccia import init
from agents import Agent, Runner

init()  # Automatically enables Agents SDK tracing

agent = Agent(
    name="Assistant",
    instructions="You are a helpful assistant"
)
result = Runner.run_sync(agent, "Write a haiku about recursion")
```

Configuration: Auto-enabled by default when `openai-agents` is installed. To disable:

```
init(openai_agents=False)  # Explicit parameter
# OR set environment variable: TRACCIA_OPENAI_AGENTS=false
# OR in traccia.toml under [instrumentation]: openai_agents = false
```

Compatibility: If you have `openai-agents` installed but don't use it (e.g., using LangChain or pure OpenAI instead), the integration is registered but never invoked—no overhead or extra spans.

### CrewAI

Traccia automatically instruments CrewAI when it is installed in your environment.

```
from traccia import init
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew, Process

init()  # Auto-enables CrewAI tracing when CrewAI is installed

researcher = Agent(role="Research Analyst", goal="Research a topic", llm="gpt-4o-mini")
task = Task(description="Research Shawn Michaels", agent=researcher)

crew = Crew(agents=[researcher], tasks=[task], process=Process.sequential, verbose=True)
result = crew.kickoff()
```

Traccia will create spans for the crew (`crewai.crew.kickoff`), each task (`crewai.task.*`), agents (`crewai.agent.*`), and underlying LLM calls, which nest under the existing OpenAI spans.

Configuration: Auto-enabled by default when `crewai` is installed. To disable:

```
init(crewai=False)  # Explicit parameter
# OR set environment variable: TRACCIA_CREWAI=false
# OR in traccia.toml under [instrumentation]: crewai = false
```

## 🛡️ Guardrail Detection

Traccia includes a passive guardrail detection engine that runs as a span processor — no runtime enforcement, no changes required to existing agent code. It inspects every span as it ends, classifies guardrail signals into structured findings, and writes results back onto spans so they appear in any configured exporter.

### How it works

Detection is automatic once `traccia.init()` is called. The processor runs three tiers against every span's attributes:

| Tier | Source | Confidence | How |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A — Explicit | `explicit` | `high` | `@observe(as_type="guardrail")` or `guardrail_span()` |
| B — Provider-native | `provider_native` | `high`/`medium` | LLM finish reason, stop reason, safety ratings |
| C — Heuristic | `heuristic` | always `low` | Denial keywords in tool error messages |

At the end of each trace (when the root span ends), the processor evaluates which guardrail categories should exist given the agent's observed capabilities (LLM calls, tool use, user-provided text) and reports which are missing.

### Annotating guardrails explicitly (Tier A)

Option 1: `guardrail_span` context manager — recommended for inline checks

```
from traccia.guardrails import guardrail_span

with guardrail_span("pii_check", category="pii", enforcement_mode="warn") as span:
    result = run_pii_check(user_input)
    span.set_attribute("guardrail.triggered", result.found_pii)
```

Option 2: `@observe(as_type="guardrail")` decorator — for function-level guardrails

If your guardrail function returns a `bool`, `guardrail.triggered` is set automatically:

```
from traccia import observe

@observe(
    as_type="guardrail",
    attributes={
        "guardrail.name": "prompt_injection_check",
        "guardrail.category": "prompt_injection",
        "guardrail.enforcement_mode": "block",
    }
)
def check_injection(text: str) -> bool:
    return any(kw in text.lower() for kw in INJECTION_KEYWORDS)
    # True → triggered (blocked), False → not triggered
```

For non-bool returns, set `guardrail.triggered` manually on the current span.

### Suppressing false positive missing-guardrail warnings

Batch pipelines or internal-only agents often get flagged for `prompt_injection` / `input_validation` because they make LLM calls with `llm.prompt`. Suppress specific categories for a run:

```
from traccia.guardrails import guardrail_span

# Convenience: suppress_missing on guardrail_span
with guardrail_span("root", category="unknown", suppress_missing=["prompt_injection", "input_validation"]):
    run_batch_pipeline()

# Or directly on any span
from traccia.guardrails import ATTR_GUARDRAIL_SUPPRESS_MISSING
span.set_attribute(ATTR_GUARDRAIL_SUPPRESS_MISSING, ["prompt_injection"])
```

### What appears in traces

Per span (when a guardrail signal is found):

- `guardrail.finding.count` — number of findings on this span
- `guardrail.findings` — JSON array of `GuardrailFinding` objects

On the root span (aggregated summary of the entire run):

- `guardrail.summary` — full `GuardrailSummary` JSON
- `guardrail.summary.coverage_confidence` — `"high"`, `"medium"`, or `"low"`
- `guardrail.summary.missing_count` — number of expected-but-missing guardrail categories
- `guardrail.summary.detected_categories` — list of detected category strings

### Provider-native detection (Tier B, automatic)

These signals are detected automatically from LLM span attributes — no annotation required:

| Provider | Signal | Attribute |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI | `finish_reason = "content_filter"` | `llm.finish_reason` |
| Azure OpenAI | `finish_reason = "content_filtered"` | `llm.finish_reason` |
| Google GenAI | `finish_reason = "SAFETY"` | `llm.finish_reason` |
| Anthropic | `stop_reason = "content_filter"` | `llm.stop_reason` |
| Anthropic | Policy violation error message | `error.message` + `llm.vendor=anthropic` |
| Google/LangChain | `"blocked": true` or `"probability": "HIGH"` in safety ratings | `llm.safety_ratings` |

### Disabling Tier C (heuristic) detection

Tier A/B stay on. Turn off tool-error keyword heuristics if you do not want Tier C at all:

```
init(guardrail_heuristics=False)
```

Or `TRACCIA_GUARDRAIL_HEURISTICS=false`, or in `traccia.toml`: `[instrumentation]` → `guardrail_heuristics = false`.

### Hard limits — what cannot be captured

- Guardrails running outside the traced process (API gateways, proxies, external validators) are invisible unless they write span attributes.
- A guardrail that exists but never fires cannot be distinguished from a missing guardrail. Only explicit annotation proves presence.
- Prompt injection detection requires an explicit span — the model's output alone cannot reliably indicate whether a check ran.
- Capability inference (`handles_user_text`) is inferred from `llm.prompt` being present; batch pipelines and user-facing agents look the same. Use suppression to opt out.

### Configuration Precedence

Traccia merges configuration from multiple sources with the following priority (highest to lowest):

1. Explicit parameters — `init(endpoint="...", agent_id="...")` or `start_tracing(...)`
2. Environment variables — `TRACCIA_ENDPOINT`, `TRACCIA_AGENT_ID`, etc.
3. Config file — `traccia.toml` (current directory) or `~/.traccia/config.toml`
4. Defaults — Built-in SDK defaults

Example: If you set `TRACCIA_ENDPOINT` in your environment and pass `endpoint=...` to `init()`, the explicit parameter wins.

### Configuration File

Create a `traccia.toml` file in your project root:

```
traccia config init
```

This creates a template config file:

```
[tracing]
# API key — required for the Traccia platform, not needed for local OTLP backends
api_key = ""

# Endpoint URL for OTLP trace ingestion (default: Traccia platform)
# For local OTLP backends use e.g. endpoint = "http://localhost:4318/v1/traces"
endpoint = "https://api.traccia.ai/v2/traces"

sample_rate = 1.0           # 0.0 to 1.0
auto_start_trace = true     # Auto-start root trace on init
auto_trace_name = "root"    # Name for auto-started trace
use_otlp = true             # Use OTLP exporter
# service_name = "my-app"   # Optional service name
# service_role has no env var — pass via init(service_role="orchestrator")

[exporters]
# Only enable ONE exporter at a time
enable_console = false        # Print traces to console
enable_file = false           # Write traces to file
file_exporter_path = "traces.jsonl"
reset_trace_file = false      # Reset file on initialization

[instrumentation]
enable_patching = true          # Auto-patch libraries (OpenAI, Anthropic, requests)
enable_token_counting = true    # Count tokens for LLM calls
enable_costs = true             # Calculate costs
openai_agents = true            # Auto-enable OpenAI Agents SDK integration
crewai = true                   # Auto-enable CrewAI integration
guardrail_heuristics = true     # Tier C heuristic guardrail detection (tool error keywords)
auto_instrument_tools = false   # Auto-instrument tool calls (experimental)
max_tool_spans = 100            # Max tool spans to create
max_span_depth = 10             # Max nested span depth

[rate_limiting]
# Optional: limit spans per second
# max_spans_per_second = 100.0
max_queue_size = 5000           # Max buffered spans
max_block_ms = 100              # Max ms to block before dropping
max_export_batch_size = 512     # Spans per export batch
schedule_delay_millis = 5000    # Delay between batches

[metrics]
enable_metrics = true           # Enable OpenTelemetry metrics
# metrics_endpoint = ""         # Defaults to {traces_base}/v2/metrics
metrics_sample_rate = 1.0       # Metrics sampling rate (1.0 = 100%)

[runtime]
# Optional runtime metadata (agent identity: prefer init(agent_id=..., agent_name=..., env=...) or TRACCIA_* env)
# session_id = ""
# user_id = ""
# tenant_id = ""
# project_id = ""
# agent_id = ""   # Single-agent: set in code or TRACCIA_AGENT_ID
# agent_name = ""
# env = ""        # e.g. production, staging, dev

[logging]
debug = false                   # Enable debug logging
enable_span_logging = false     # Enable span-level logging

[advanced]
# attr_truncation_limit = 1000  # Max attribute value length
```

### Default endpoint

If you do not set `endpoint` (in config, environment, or when calling `init()` / `start_tracing()`), the SDK uses the Traccia platform by default (`https://api.traccia.ai/v2/traces`). You can override it to send traces to your own OTLP-compatible backend.

The default is defined in `traccia.config`: `DEFAULT_OTLP_TRACE_ENDPOINT`. The alias `DEFAULT_ENDPOINT` is kept for backward compatibility (same value).

### OTLP Backend Compatibility

Traccia is fully OTLP-compatible and works with:

- Grafana Tempo - `http://tempo:4318/v1/traces`
- Jaeger - `http://jaeger:4318/v1/traces`
- Zipkin - Configure via OTLP endpoint
- SigNoz - Self-hosted observability platform
- Traccia Platform - `https://api.traccia.ai/v2/traces` (requires API key)

### Environment Variables

All config parameters can be set via environment variables with the `TRACCIA_` prefix:

Tracing: `TRACCIA_API_KEY`, `TRACCIA_ENDPOINT`, `TRACCIA_SAMPLE_RATE`, `TRACCIA_AUTO_START_TRACE`, `TRACCIA_AUTO_TRACE_NAME`, `TRACCIA_USE_OTLP`, `TRACCIA_SERVICE_NAME`

Exporters: `TRACCIA_ENABLE_CONSOLE`, `TRACCIA_ENABLE_FILE`, `TRACCIA_FILE_PATH`, `TRACCIA_RESET_TRACE_FILE`

Instrumentation: `TRACCIA_ENABLE_PATCHING`, `TRACCIA_ENABLE_TOKEN_COUNTING`, `TRACCIA_ENABLE_COSTS`, `TRACCIA_AUTO_INSTRUMENT_TOOLS`, `TRACCIA_MAX_TOOL_SPANS`, `TRACCIA_MAX_SPAN_DEPTH`, `TRACCIA_OPENAI_AGENTS`, `TRACCIA_CREWAI`, `TRACCIA_GUARDRAIL_HEURISTICS`

Rate Limiting: `TRACCIA_MAX_SPANS_PER_SECOND`, `TRACCIA_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE`, `TRACCIA_MAX_BLOCK_MS`, `TRACCIA_MAX_EXPORT_BATCH_SIZE`, `TRACCIA_SCHEDULE_DELAY_MILLIS`

Runtime: `TRACCIA_SESSION_ID`, `TRACCIA_USER_ID`, `TRACCIA_TENANT_ID`, `TRACCIA_PROJECT_ID`, `TRACCIA_AGENT_ID`, `TRACCIA_AGENT_NAME`, `TRACCIA_ENV`

Legacy alias: `TRACCIA_PROJECT` (maps to `project_id`)

Logging: `TRACCIA_DEBUG`, `TRACCIA_ENABLE_SPAN_LOGGING`

Advanced: `TRACCIA_ATTR_TRUNCATION_LIMIT`

### Programmatic Configuration

```
from traccia import init

# Override config programmatically (including agent identity for single-agent services)
init(
    endpoint="http://tempo:4318/v1/traces",
    sample_rate=0.5,
    enable_costs=True,
    max_spans_per_second=100.0,
    agent_id="my-agent",
    agent_name="My Agent",
    env="production",
)
```

### Multi-Agent Orchestrator Services

For services that orchestrate many logical agents in one process, set a service role and scope per-run identity:

```
from traccia import init, runtime_config

init(
    service_name="my-multi-agent-api",
    service_role="orchestrator",
    auto_start_trace=False,
)

with runtime_config.run_identity(agent_id="billing-agent", agent_name="Billing Agent", env="production"):
    # run one logical agent task
    ...
```

This prevents the host service from being registered as a synthetic agent in the Traccia platform.

### Safe Parallel Runs in One Process

If one process runs many agents concurrently (for example, an API server or orchestrator), use this pattern:

- Call `init()` once per process (for example at startup), not per request.
- Wrap each logical "run" in `runtime_config.run_identity(...)` to set agent id/name/env for that run.
- Do not call `stop_tracing()` per request; use `force_flush()` to flush spans/metrics after a run without shutting down the provider.

```
from traccia import init, span, force_flush, runtime_config

init(service_name="multi-agent-service", auto_start_trace=False)

def run_agent(agent_id: str, env: str, payload: dict):
    # Scope identity to this run only
    with runtime_config.run_identity(agent_id=agent_id, agent_name=agent_id, env=env):
        with span("agent.run") as root:
            root.set_attribute("agent.id", agent_id)
            root.set_attribute("agent.run.mode", "api")
            # ... your agent logic here ...

    # Flush without tearing down the global provider
    force_flush(5.0)
```

### The `@observe` Decorator

The `@observe` decorator is the primary way to instrument your code:

```
from traccia import observe

# Basic usage
@observe()
def process_data(data):
    return transform(data)

# Custom span name
@observe(name="data_pipeline")
def process_data(data):
    return transform(data)

# Add custom attributes
@observe(attributes={"version": "2.0", "env": "prod"})
def process_data(data):
    return transform(data)

# Specify span type
@observe(as_type="llm")  # "span", "llm", "tool"
def call_llm():
    pass

# Skip capturing specific arguments
@observe(skip_args=["password", "secret"])
def authenticate(username, password):
    pass

# Skip capturing result (for large returns)
@observe(skip_result=True)
def fetch_large_dataset():
    return huge_data
```

Available Parameters:

- `name` (str, optional): Custom span name (defaults to function name)
- `attributes` (dict, optional): Initial span attributes
- `as_type` (str): Span type - `"span"`, `"llm"`, `"tool"`, or `"guardrail"`
- `skip_args` (list, optional): List of argument names to skip capturing
- `skip_result` (bool): Skip capturing the return value

### Async Functions

`@observe` works seamlessly with async functions:

```
@observe()
async def async_task(x):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return x * 2

result = await async_task(5)
```

### Manual Span Creation

For more control, create spans manually:

```
from traccia import get_tracer, span

# Using convenience function
with span("operation_name") as s:
    s.set_attribute("key", "value")
    s.add_event("checkpoint_reached")
    do_work()

# Using tracer directly
tracer = get_tracer("my_service")
with tracer.start_as_current_span("operation") as s:
    s.set_attribute("user_id", 123)
    do_work()
```

### Error Handling

Traccia automatically captures and records errors:

```
@observe()
def failing_function():
    raise ValueError("Something went wrong")

# Span will contain:
# - error.type: "ValueError"
# - error.message: "Something went wrong"
# - error.stack_trace: (truncated stack trace)
# - span status: ERROR
```

### Nested Spans

Spans are automatically nested based on call hierarchy:

```
@observe()
def parent_operation():
    child_operation()
    return "done"

@observe()
def child_operation():
    grandchild_operation()

@observe()
def grandchild_operation():
    pass

# Creates nested span hierarchy:
# parent_operation
#   └── child_operation
#       └── grandchild_operation
```

## 🛠️ CLI Tools

Traccia includes a powerful CLI for configuration and diagnostics:

### `traccia config init`

Create a new `traccia.toml` configuration file:

```
traccia config init
traccia config init --force  # Overwrite existing
```

### `traccia doctor`

Validate configuration and diagnose issues:

```
traccia doctor

# Output:
# 🩺 Running Traccia configuration diagnostics...
# 
# ✅ Found config file: ./traccia.toml
# ✅ Configuration is valid
# 
# 📊 Configuration summary:
#    • API Key: ❌ Not set (optional)
#    • Endpoint: https://api.traccia.ai/v2/traces
#    • Sample Rate: 1.0
#    • OTLP Exporter: ✅ Enabled
```

### `traccia check`

Test connectivity to your exporter endpoint:

```
traccia check
traccia check --endpoint http://tempo:4318/v1/traces
```

### Rate Limiting

Protect your infrastructure with built-in rate limiting:

```
[rate_limiting]
max_spans_per_second = 100.0  # Limit to 100 spans/sec
max_queue_size = 5000         # Max buffered spans
max_block_ms = 100             # Block up to 100ms before dropping
```

Behavior:

1. Try to acquire capacity immediately
2. If unavailable, block for up to `max_block_ms`
3. If still unavailable, drop span and log warning

When spans are dropped due to rate limiting, warnings are logged to help you monitor and adjust limits.

### Sampling

Control trace volume with sampling:

```
# Sample 10% of traces
init(sample_rate=0.1)

# Sampling is applied at trace creation time
# Traces are either fully included or fully excluded
```

### Token Counting & Cost Calculation

Automatic for supported LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic):

```
@observe(as_type="llm")
def call_openai(prompt):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

# Span automatically includes:
# - llm.token.prompt_tokens
# - llm.token.completion_tokens
# - llm.token.total_tokens
# - llm.cost.total (in USD)
```

### Metrics

Traccia emits OTEL-compliant metrics for accurate cost and token tracking, independent of trace sampling.

#### Why Metrics?

With trace sampling (e.g., `sample_rate=0.1`), only 10% of traces are exported. Cost calculated from traces will be 10x underestimated. Metrics solve this by recording data for every LLM call, regardless of sampling.

#### Default Metrics

Traccia automatically emits these metrics:

| Metric | Type | Unit | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gen_ai.client.token.usage` | Histogram | `{token}` | Input/output tokens per call |
| `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` | Histogram | `s` | LLM operation duration |
| `gen_ai.client.operation.cost` | Histogram | `usd` | Cost per call (USD) |
| `gen_ai.client.completions.exceptions` | Counter | `1` | Exception count |
| `gen_ai.agent.runs` | Counter | `1` | Agent runs (CrewAI, OpenAI Agents) |
| `gen_ai.agent.turns` | Counter | `1` | Agent turns |
| `gen_ai.agent.execution_time` | Histogram | `s` | Agent execution time |

Attributes: `gen_ai.system` (openai, anthropic), `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.agent.id`, `gen_ai.agent.name`

#### Configuration

```
from traccia import init

init(
    enable_metrics=True,  # Default: True
    metrics_endpoint="https://your-backend.com/v2/metrics",  
    metrics_sample_rate=1.0,  # Default: 1.0 (100%)
)
```

Or via `traccia.toml`:

```
[metrics]
enable_metrics = true
metrics_endpoint = "https://your-backend.com/v2/metrics"
metrics_sample_rate = 1.0
```

Or via environment variables:

```
export TRACCIA_ENABLE_METRICS=true
export TRACCIA_METRICS_ENDPOINT=https://your-backend.com/v2/metrics
export TRACCIA_METRICS_SAMPLE_RATE=1.0
```

#### Custom Metrics

Record your own metrics:

```
from traccia.metrics import record_counter, record_histogram

# Record a counter
record_counter("my_custom_events", 1, {"event_type": "user_action"})

# Record a histogram
record_histogram("my_custom_latency", 0.123, {"service": "api"}, unit="s")
```

#### Agent Metrics vs. Plain LLM Calls

Agent-level metrics (such as `gen_ai.agent.runs` and `gen_ai.agent.execution_time`) are only emitted when Traccia can see a real agent lifecycle (for example, CrewAI crews or OpenAI Agents SDK runs). For plain OpenAI/Anthropic calls and most simple LangChain usages, you will still get full LLM metrics (`gen_ai.client.*`), but no agent metrics unless you build an explicit agent abstraction on top.

### Enable Debug Logging

```
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

# Or via config
init(debug=True)

# Or via env var
# TRACCIA_DEBUG=1 python your_script.py
```

#### Traces not appearing

1. Check connectivity: `traccia check`
2. Validate config: `traccia doctor`
3. Enable debug logging
4. Verify endpoint is correct and accessible

#### High memory usage

- Reduce `max_queue_size` in rate limiting config
- Lower `sample_rate` to reduce volume
- Enable rate limiting with `max_spans_per_second`

#### Spans being dropped

- Check rate limiter logs for warnings
- Increase `max_spans_per_second` if set
- Increase `max_queue_size` if spans are queued
- Check `traccia doctor` output

#### `init(**kwargs) -> TracerProvider`

Initialize the Traccia SDK. All parameters are optional; configuration is merged from `traccia.toml` → env vars → explicit parameters (highest wins).

- `endpoint` (str): OTLP endpoint URL (default: `https://api.traccia.ai/v2/traces`)
- `api_key` (str): API key for the Traccia platform
- `sample_rate` (float): Sampling rate 0.0–1.0 (default: 1.0)
- `auto_start_trace` (bool): Auto-start a root trace on init (default: True)
- `auto_trace_name` (str): Name for the auto-started trace (default: `"root"`)
- `use_otlp` (bool): Use OTLP exporter (default: True)
- `service_name` (str): Service name (auto-detected if not set)
- `service_role` (str): `"orchestrator"` to prevent this service being registered as an agent
- `config_file` (str): Path to a custom `traccia.toml`

- `enable_console_exporter` (bool): Print spans to stdout (default: False)
- `enable_file_exporter` (bool): Write spans to file (default: False)
- `file_exporter_path` (str): Path for file exporter (default: `"traces.jsonl"`)
- `reset_trace_file` (bool): Clear file on init (default: False)

- `enable_patching` (bool): Auto-patch OpenAI, Anthropic, requests (default: True)
- `enable_token_counting` (bool): Count tokens (default: True)
- `enable_costs` (bool): Calculate costs (default: True)
- `openai_agents` (bool): Auto-enable OpenAI Agents SDK integration (default: True)
- `crewai` (bool): Auto-enable CrewAI integration (default: True)
- `guardrail_heuristics` (bool): Enable Tier C heuristic guardrail detection (default: True)
- `auto_instrument_tools` (bool): Experimental tool auto-instrumentation (default: False)
- `max_tool_spans` (int): Max tool spans per trace (default: 100)
- `max_span_depth` (int): Max nested span depth (default: 10)

Agent identity (single-agent services)

- `agent_id` (str): Logical agent identifier
- `agent_name` (str): Human-readable agent name
- `env` (str): Deployment environment, e.g. `"production"`, `"staging"`

- `session_id` (str): Session identifier
- `user_id` (str): User identifier
- `tenant_id` (str): Tenant / org identifier
- `project_id` (str): Project identifier

- `enable_metrics` (bool): Emit OTEL metrics (default: True)
- `metrics_endpoint` (str): Metrics endpoint (derived from tracing endpoint if not set)
- `metrics_sample_rate` (float): Metrics sampling rate (default: 1.0)

Rate limiting

- `max_spans_per_second` (float): Rate limit spans/sec (default: None = unlimited)
- `max_block_ms` (int): Max ms to block before dropping a span (default: 100)
- `max_queue_size` (int): Max buffered spans (default: 5000)
- `max_export_batch_size` (int): Spans per export batch (default: 512)
- `schedule_delay_millis` (int): Batch export interval ms (default: 5000)

- `debug` (bool): Enable debug logging (default: False)
- `attr_truncation_limit` (int): Max attribute value length (default: None)

#### `stop_tracing(flush_timeout: float = 1.0) -> None`

Stop tracing and flush pending spans.

- `flush_timeout` (float): Max seconds to wait for flush

#### `get_tracer(name: str = "default") -> Tracer`

Get a tracer instance.

- `name` (str): Tracer name (typically module/service name)

#### `span(name: str, attributes: dict = None) -> Span`

Create a span context manager.

- `name` (str): Span name
- `attributes` (dict, optional): Initial attributes

Returns: Span context manager

#### `@observe(name=None, *, attributes=None, tags=None, as_type="span", skip_args=None, skip_result=False)`

Decorate a function to create spans automatically.

- `name` (str, optional): Span name (default: function name)
- `attributes` (dict, optional): Initial attributes
- `tags` (list[str], optional): User-defined identifiers for the observed method
- `as_type` (str): Span type (`"span"`, `"llm"`, `"tool"`, `"guardrail"`)
- `skip_args` (list, optional): Arguments to skip capturing
- `skip_result` (bool): Skip capturing return value

#### `load_config(config_file=None, overrides=None) -> TracciaConfig`

Load and validate configuration.

- `config_file` (str, optional): Path to config file
- `overrides` (dict, optional): Override values

Returns: Validated TracciaConfig instance

Raises: `ConfigError` if invalid

#### `validate_config(config_file=None, overrides=None) -> tuple[bool, str, TracciaConfig | None]`

Validate configuration without loading.

Returns: Tuple of (is_valid, message, config_or_none)

### Data Flow

```
Application Code (@observe)
        ↓
   Span Creation
        ↓
   Processors (token counting, cost, enrichment)
        ↓
   Rate Limiter (optional)
        ↓
   Batch Processor (buffering)
        ↓
   Exporter (OTLP/Console/File)
        ↓
   Backend (Grafana Tempo / Jaeger / Zipkin / etc.)

```

### Instrumentation vs Integrations

- `traccia.instrumentation.*`: Infrastructure and vendor instrumentation.

- HTTP client/server helpers (including FastAPI middleware).
- Vendor SDK hooks and monkey patching (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, `requests`).
- Decorators and utilities used for auto-instrumenting arbitrary functions.
- `traccia.integrations.*`: AI/agent framework integrations.

- Adapters that plug into higher-level frameworks via their official extension points (e.g., LangChain callbacks).
- Work at the level of chains, tools, agents, and workflows rather than raw HTTP or SDK calls.

## 🤝 Contributing

Contributions are welcome! Whether it's bug fixes, new features, documentation improvements, or examples - we appreciate your help.

### How to Contribute

1. Fork the repository
2. Create a feature branch: `git checkout -b feature/amazing-feature`
3. Make your changes and add tests
4. Run tests: `pytest traccia/tests/`
5. Lint your code: `ruff check traccia/`
6. Commit: `git commit -m "Add amazing feature"`
7. Push: `git push origin feature/amazing-feature`
8. Open a Pull Request

### Development Setup

```
# Clone the repository (Python SDK)
git clone https://github.com/traccia-ai/traccia-py.git
cd traccia-py

# Create virtual environment
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate  # On Windows: venv\Scripts\activate

# Install in editable mode with dev dependencies
pip install -e ".[dev]"

# Run tests
pytest traccia/tests/ -v

# Run with coverage
pytest traccia/tests/ --cov=traccia --cov-report=html
```

### Code Style

- Follow PEP 8
- Use type hints where appropriate
- Add docstrings for public APIs
- Write tests for new features
- Keep PRs focused and atomic

### Areas We'd Love Help With

- Integrations: Add support for more LLM providers (Cohere, AI21, local models)
- Backends: Test and document setup with different OTLP backends
- Examples: Real-world examples of agent instrumentation
- Documentation: Tutorials, guides, video walkthroughs
- Performance: Optimize hot paths, reduce overhead
- Testing: Improve test coverage, add integration tests

Inspired by observability tools in the ecosystem and designed to work seamlessly with the OTLP standard.

title: Show HN: HackerByte – Finding promising AI stories by analyzing HN discussions
author: bakigul
body: This was something I wanted to build for a long time.AI news is moving so fast now. Every day there are new projects, tools and updates. It's hard to follow everything, and we don't always have time to read long articles.So I built HackerByte. It takes Hacker News stories and makes short summaries in 6-7 sentences. You can quickly understand what's going on without reading everything. I also added the same thing for GitHub Trending projects.I also added a feature that analyzes HN comments to find AI stories that might be worth checking out.In the future, I want to add some personalization features, so everyone can see content based on their interests.I've been a software developer for 7 years, and of course I didn't write a single line of code myself while building this :)After seeing Karpathy share HackerTube, I thought, why not build my own version? So I did.I'd love to hear your feedback!https://hackerbyte.net/

title: Show HN: Confetti – Start designing hardware with plain English prompts
author: enaic

author: craigm26
body:
Skip to content 
 graftfork is now in Claude's connector directory. Connect it in Claude → 
graftfork 
 Try it How it works Rebuilds Pricing Teams Docs Security FAQ Changelog 
 Sign in Sign up free 
Try it, no sign-up
See what Graft would do with your fork
Paste a public GitHub fork, or any copy of an open-source project with your changes as commits on a release. Graft moves your changes onto upstream's newest release in a sandbox, runs your tests, and shows you the change it would deliver.
Try it 
Trying a fork is closed until Graft opens, for everyone. Your dashboard works: connect your copy in Copies , or rebuild a program from its spec in Specs .
No fork to hand? Try a real one, in one click:
pattonw/tqdm Python, moves clarketm/pflag Go, moves sigmavirus24/requests moves guyernest/arrow stays, and says why 
What a try does
Finds the facts. The upstream (a fork's parent, or the project your files name), the release your changes sit on, how many changes are yours, and upstream's newest release. 
Moves your changes in a sandbox. A short-lived sandbox (a Claude Managed Agents container on Anthropic, deleted within minutes of the try ending) clones your public fork, carries each change onto the newest release, and runs your tests if it finds them (Python and Node projects, or a .graft.yml ). 
Tells you what happened. Each change kept, dropped because the release already has it, or conflicting; the tests' verdict; and the change Graft would deliver, with its diff. You watch each change decided as it happens, and you can share the result: its link, a card image, or a post to X or LinkedIn. 
What it can't do
Push. A try has no access to your repository beyond a public clone, no write token ever enters its sandbox, and the runner refuses to push a try whatever it's told. 
Use an agent. A try runs the no-agent path. A conflict is shown as a conflict. Once you're connected, Premium resolves conflicts automatically, your first one is free, or you can use your own Anthropic key. 
Run long. Ten minutes at most, up to ten tries running at once and fifty more waiting in line, ten tries a day per visitor (people on one network share them). Public repositories only. A result for the same fork and release is reused for 24 hours. 
We keep the result, the repository's name and a salted hash of your IP address (for the limits) for 30 days, then delete them. See privacy .
graftfork Keep your changes. Keep getting updates. Never move onto a copy that fails your tests. Graft carries your changes to an open-source project onto each new release and delivers the moved branch only when your tests pass; it can also rebuild a program from its spec.

title: Show HN: An MCP proxy that sends 97% fewer tool-definition tokens per request
author: TDabasinskas
body:
# datolabs-io/mcp-toolsearch-proxy

MCP server that puts search_tools, describe_tool and the call tools in front of a large MCP tool catalog

- Stars: 1
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 1
- Open issues: 2
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-30T15:26:35Z

## Languages

- Dockerfile
- Go
- Shell

## Topics

- go
- mcp
- mcp-server
- model-context-protocol
- tool-search

## Top Contributors

- tdabasinskas (7 contributions)
- datolabs-automation[bot] (3 contributions)
- renovate[bot] (2 contributions)

---

## README

# mcp-toolsearch-proxy

CI
OpenSSF Scorecard
Glama

**mcp-toolsearch-proxy** lets a model use hundreds or thousands of MCP tools without loading them. On 500 tools, each
request carries 97% fewer tokens of tool definitions, a task costs about half as much, and the model reaches the right
tool nearly as often as with every tool loaded (benchmarks).

It is an MCP server that puts five tools in front of an MCP server with far too many
to list to a model, such as a gateway that aggregates dozens of servers:

| Tool | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `search_tools` | finds the tools that can do what a query describes, with the input schemas of the best few, for up to 5 queries at once; with the built-in model, in English, Lithuanian or any of 100 other languages |
| `describe_tool` | returns the full description and input schema of up to 10 tools |
| `call_read_tool` | calls a tool the upstream marks read-only, and refuses any other |
| `call_read_tools` | calls up to 10 read-only tools at once, in parallel, with a result for each (`-max-batch-calls`; 0 leaves it out) |
| `call_write_tool` | calls any tool, for those that may create, change or delete something |

A catalog of a thousand tools costs a model over 100,000 tokens of tool definitions before it does anything, and many
clients cap how many tools they load anyway. Behind the proxy, the model sees five, in 1,735 tokens.

A call whose arguments do not fit the tool's input schema (a required property missing, a wrong type, a value outside
an enum) is refused before it reaches the upstream, with what is wrong and the schema, so the model can fix it at once.
The same goes for an unknown name that is clearly a typo of one tool, and for an upstream that answers invalid params.

Calls come in separate tools so that a client can tell them apart: `call_read_tool` and `call_read_tools` are marked
read-only and can be allowed to run without asking, while `call_write_tool` is marked destructive and can keep asking
every time. Writes are never batched, so each keeps its own approval. A tool counts as
read-only only when the upstream server marks it so (`readOnlyHint`); unmarked tools are writes, and so are any the
operator lists in `-write-tools`. Allowing `call_read_tool` allows every read-only tool of every server behind the
upstream, including servers added later; docs/clients.md says what that grant covers and how to set
up claude.ai and Claude Code.

```text
client ──▶ gateway /mcp/search ──▶ mcp-toolsearch-proxy ──▶ gateway /mcp/all ──▶ MCP servers
```

## How it works

The proxy has no credentials. Each request it sends upstream carries the caller's `Authorization` header and nothing
else, so the upstream server (usually the same gateway, on another route) authenticates and authorizes the caller as
if they had come directly. Whatever the caller isn't allowed to see or call, the proxy can't see or call either.

Each caller gets their own catalog: the tools the upstream lists for that caller. It is kept for ten minutes, then
listed again in the background while the old one is still used, and it is looked up by a hash of the token. A claim
inside the token, such as `sub`, would be easier to key on but can't be trusted without verifying the token, so the
proxy doesn't use one.

Search combines two rankings. BM25 matches words in tool names, descriptions and parameters, with Lithuanian and
English endings stemmed and diacritics ignored. A multilingual embedding model,
potion-multilingual-128M (MIT), matches by meaning. The
model runs inside the proxy, in pure Go, without a GPU or an embedding service, and embedding a query takes
microseconds. Without the model, search falls back to BM25 alone, which matches only words a tool's text shares with
the query: it stems no endings but Lithuanian and English ones, and does not split Chinese or Japanese text into words.

The upstream server's own instructions still reach the model. The proxy answers each caller's handshake with its own
short guidance followed by the upstream's `instructions`, unchanged, as the caller's catalog received them, up to
`-max-instructions` characters (10,000 by default; longer ones are cut, with a note saying so). Clients cut it again,
much sooner: Claude Code keeps about 4,000 characters of a server's instructions, so only the start of a long upstream
text reaches the model (see docs/clients.md). And `search_tools`
returns the input schemas of its best few matches (`-search-schemas`, 3 by default), so a call usually follows a
search directly.

Logs and metrics record tool names, outcomes and timings. Queries, arguments, results and tokens never appear in
them; docs/privacy.md has the details. The transport is streamable HTTP without sessions, for
MCP 2026-07-28 clients and older ones, so a restart or a load balancer doesn't break a client's connection.
`-transport stdio` serves the same tools on standard input and output instead, for clients that start servers as local
commands. There is no caller's token there, and the proxy has none of its own, so stdio works only with an upstream
that needs no authentication (docs/clients.md).

It works with any upstream that speaks streamable HTTP MCP and authorizes by bearer token.
docs/agentgateway.md shows a complete agentgateway setup, which
the end-to-end tests run.

## Status

Early development. The tools, their arguments and the settings may still change before 1.0.

## Install

Homebrew, on macOS or Linux:

```bash
brew install --cask datolabs-io/tap/mcp-toolsearch-proxy
```

Packages (`.deb`, `.rpm`), archives and a container image are attached to each
release. See docs/deploy.md.

```bash
mcp-toolsearch-proxy fetch-model -model-dir ./model        # once: ~530 MB, checked against pinned digests
mcp-toolsearch-proxy -upstream https://gateway.example.com/mcp/all -model-dir ./model
```

`-embedder none` skips the model and searches lexically only. docs/configuration.md lists
every setting, as `mcp-toolsearch-proxy -h` does; each has an environment variable too. Then connect a client:
docs/clients.md.

Clients that already defer MCP tools and search them on demand, as Claude Code does, gain less from the proxy; see
when you don't need this.

## Search quality

The repository holds an evaluation set of made-up tools, described in English, and questions people ask about them
in English and Lithuanian. Recall at 5 today:

| Search | English | Lithuanian |
| --- | --- | --- |
| lexical only (`-embedder none`) | 52% | 0% |
| hybrid with the built-in model | 81% | 79% |

Words alone can't connect a Lithuanian question to an English description. The model can. Tests hold changes to
ranking to these numbers.

## Benchmarks

On a made-up catalog of 500 tools, a model given 30 questions reaches the right tool nearly as often through the proxy
(90%) as with every tool loaded (95%), at about half the cost per task, and more often than with Anthropic's tool
search (87%). docs/benchmarks.md has the numbers, what a client loads in each mode at up to 1,490
tools, and how to run the benchmarks.

## Development

```bash
mise install          # the pinned toolchain and the git hooks
mise run ci           # lint, scan and unit tests, as CI runs them
mise run test:model   # the built-in model against its reference implementation and the evaluation set
mise run e2e:up       # agentgateway, the proxy and fixture MCP servers, with Docker Compose
mise run test:e2e     # the end-to-end tests, against that stack or any at E2E_SEARCH_URL and E2E_ALL_URL
mise run docs:config  # regenerate docs/configuration.md after changing a flag
```

See CONTRIBUTING.md and ARCHITECTURE.md.

## Licence

MIT. The built-in model is published by Minish under the MIT licence and is downloaded, not distributed,
by this project.

title: Show HN: I got tired of GitHub trending, so I built my own

I like to see what new projects people are working on in open-source, but I found it hard to find projects or news in any systematic way.I built Shadowgraph so that I could browse the latest in open source development in a more natural way. It ingests repos from github and scrapes hackernews, reddit, and X for mentions of them.I also identify noteworthy contributors on github and track what they're starring as a signal for potentially high quality projects that might otherwise fly under the radar. I also track their tweets or hackernews contributions for mentions of github repos for a more curated feed of content.
Finally, there's an MCP and semantic search for repos and developers.This is a fun side project for me but I want it to be useful for people- feedback is very much appreciated.

title: Show HN: Scroll from your own skeleton to the edge of the observable universe
author: vatsaltanna
body: Hi HN!I made this to help improve visualisation for a meditation I practise where you picture leaving your body moving outward in stages until you are beyond space-time. It’s helped me get through some really tough times by putting things in perspective.You start as a skeleton by the pyramids at Giza and scroll past Earth, the planets, the stars, the Milky Way and the galaxy clusters to the edge of the observable universe.It’s built with real data - 9,096 stars (Yale Bright Star Catalogue), 43,463 galaxies (2MASS Redshift Survey), asteroids (JPL), Earth (NASA Blue Marble) and Giza (Sentinel-2). The cosmic web and the faintest galaxies are generated.Runs in the browser with three.js and WebGL 2 with no sign-up or tracking. Images are GPU-compressed and load only near their stage which cut peak GPU memory from 1.1 GB to 258 MB.Hope you have fun playing around and would love to hear what you’d like to see more of!

git clone https://github.com/drawdb-io/drawdb

git clone https://github.com/drawdb-io/drawdb

title: Show HN: Backuparr – Backups for the *ARR Stack and Plex/Jellyfin/Emby
author: rsaturns
body:
I run the *arr stack on my NAS and like the lazy bad admin I was, didn't backup the configuration files / databases etc. and proceeded to have to set this all up again when my NAS died. Needless to say this sucked. So I got started on a project to ensure I didn't have to go through this again and make it as hands off as possible. I wanted something that would collect backups on a schedule and put them somewhere else, ready in the event the worst strikes again. Doing some scouring I couldn't find anything that addressed this in the manner and scope I was looking for.Backuparr is a single Docker container with a web UI. You give it each app's URL and API key, choose where the backups go (a local folder, Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox, all through rclone), and set a schedule and how long to keep them. It currently supports Radarr, Sonarr, Lidarr, Whisparr, Prowlarr, Profilarr, Bazarr, Tdarr, SABnzbd, NZBGet, Tautulli, Jellyfin, Emby, Plex, Seerr, and LazyLibrarian.If an app has a backup API, Backuparr uses it. Emby, Plex and Seerr don't have one, so it takes a SQLite online backup of their databases from a mounted folder. All of them except Profilarr can be restored from Backuparr itself, once the service container is re-deployed.The closest existing tool I found was servarr-backup, which covers Radarr, Sonarr and Prowlarr and sends backups to S3. I wanted more apps and the destinations I actually use.Limitations: the backup archives themselves aren't encrypted. Only Backuparr's own config (API keys and passwords) and rclone credentials are. Jellyfin, Emby, Plex and Seerr need their folders mounted into the container.I built this with my coding companion du jour claude-code, along with full review, a lot of self testing, debugging, full lab synthetic tests and running it against my own stack. I’ve been using it for two months now and would love some additional feedback.Docs: https://rsaturns.github.io/backuparr/
License: AGPLv3
