Yes.
Brainiac is built from scientific papers, behavioral science books, classic psychology concepts, real marketing campaigns, and business examples.
The goal is to make useful research readable without forcing you to dig through 47-page PDFs written by people allergic to normal sentences.
03 
 How is this different from reading psychology books? 
 + 
Books usually explain the idea, often using storytelling, like A LOT.
A 230-page book can introduce you to up to 10 principles without any guidance on how to use it in your business.
Books you use when you want to go deeper. You use Brainiac when you want to make it useful.
Authenticity Effect 
04 
 How is this different from AI? 
 + 
I really, really wish AI could solve this by itself. That would save me months.
But if you’ve used AI for very niche problems, you’ve probably noticed that it can give you kinda generic/obvious ideas, or full-blown nonsense. And it does it with great confidence.
Don’t get me wrong. AI is great. You can use it instead of this website.
This website is different because it’s a shortcut to 5 years of my work, thousands of hours of digging, writing, testing, collecting, and organizing.
You get a structured vault of specific principles, research-backed effects, practical examples, stats, guides, and case studies you can browse when you’re working on a real business problem.
Also, this vault has taste.
ChatGPT sometimes says things like “leverage emotional resonance.”
Nobody needs that in their life.
05 
 Will this work for my industry? 
 + 
Most likely, yes.
The principles are universal, not specialized to one market.
They can apply to SaaS, ecommerce, agencies, info products, apps, newsletters, marketplaces, communities, coaching, services, restaurants, events, creators, and strange little internet businesses that somehow make money.
06 
 Do I need to know psychology already? 
 + 
No.
Everything is written in simple language. You don’t need academic background, behavioral science vocabulary, or a PhD in making people click buttons.
07 
 Is this about manipulation? 
 + 
No.
It’s about understanding how people make decisions, what makes them hesitate, what makes them trust, and what helps them act.
You can use psychology to make things clearer, easier, safer, and more desirable.
Don’t use it like a creep.
08 
 Will this make me a better marketer? 
 + 
If you actually use it, yes.
You’ll start seeing patterns behind good marketing instead of just staring at nice landing pages and thinking, “hmm, looks expensive.”
You’ll understand why some offers feel obvious, why some products spread, why some pages convert, and why some campaigns get ignored even when they look “expensive.”
09 
 Will this make me more creative? 
 + 
Probably.
Not in the “light a candle, speak 7 affirmations, and wait for inspiration” way.
More in the “I now have 200+ weirdest marketing campaigns in history that made a bank, and I can combine them into better ideas” way.
Good creativity usually comes from having more useful material to combine.
10 
 What if I already know marketing? 
 + 
Good.
Then you’ll probably get more out of it faster.
If you already have taste and experience, this gives you more raw material.
11 
 What if I’m a beginner? 
 + 
Also fine.
You don’t need to understand every advanced marketing concept before using this.
Use the examples and copy the logic. Build from there.
12 
 Do you keep adding new stuff? 
 + 
Yes.
The vault is updated over time with new principles, case studies, examples, frameworks, and design improvements.
Lifetime access includes future updates.
13 
 Can I expense this? 
 + 
Yes.
You should be able to download an invoice or receipt after purchase through the checkout provider.
If you need approval from your boss, I also made a short email template you can steal, edit, and send.
Email template
How to send it
14 
 Why would I need multiple accounts? 
 + 
Mostly for teams.
Everyone gets their own access and personalization. Over time, the product will get more personal, so one account may look different from another.
It’s also safer than sharing one login across a team like a cursed office USB stick.
If you don’t care about that, buy one account. No worries.
If a few people will use it, buy more and pay less per person.
Authenticity Effect + Pratfall Effect 
15 
 What’s wrong with this website? 
 + 
Honestly, a few things.
This website is over 5 years old. When I started building it, I knew almost nothing about programming. I was learning by breaking things, fixing them, breaking them again, and pretending that was a process.
Because of that, some older parts don’t feel as polished as the newer ones. Some pages have design decisions I probably wouldn’t make today. Some sections are dense. Some layouts are a bit weird. Some parts still feel like they were built by someone trying to duct-tape a big idea into WordPress.
That someone was me.
Same with the case studies.
There are cases from the very beginning that I’m honestly a little embarrassed by now. Not because I didn’t care. I cared too much. I spent 15 to 30+ hours on every case from day one.
But my knowledge was smaller back then. I didn’t understand marketing mechanics, psychology, product growth, positioning, timing, and distribution as deeply as I do now. Some older breakdowns are useful, but they don’t always match the level of the newer ones.
So yes, the archive has uneven parts.
I’m slowly improving them, rewriting old case studies, cleaning up weak sections, and making the whole thing better piece by piece.
The good part is that this product has 5+ years of work inside it.
The honest part is that you can sometimes see those 5 years.

title: Show HN: Speedrunner – Faster Startup: Python, Ruby, PHP and Node CLI Tools
author: anthonygosme
body:
# anthonyGosme/speedrunner

Makes aws, az, gcloud, ansible, eslint, rubocop, composer and hundreds of other Python, Ruby, PHP and Node CLIs start several times faster: each stays loaded in a daemon that forks it on every call. A checks script: 24.0 s → 5.3 s, same output. No per-tool config, one binary, Linux and macOS.

- Stars: 1
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 1
- Open issues: 0
- License: Apache License 2.0
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-29T01:30:59Z

## Languages

- C
- Dockerfile
- JavaScript
- PHP
- Python
- Ruby
- Rust
- Shell
- TypeScript

## Topics

- cli
- command-line
- daemon
- developer-tools
- fork
- linux
- nodejs
- performance
- php
- preload
- python
- ruby
- rust
- startup-time

## Top Contributors

- anthonyGosme (133 contributions)
- github-actions[bot] (1 contributions)

---

## README

```text
 ____                      _                                  
/ ___| _ __   ___  ___  __| |_ __ _   _ _ __  _ __   ___ _ __ 
\___ \| '_ \ / _ \/ _ \/ _` | '__| | | | '_ \| '_ \ / _ \ '__|
 ___) | |_) |  __/  __/ (_| | |  | |_| | | | | | | |  __/ |   
|____/| .__/ \___|\___|\__,_|_|   \__,_|_| |_|_| |_|\___|_|   
      |_|                                                     
```

aws, az, gcloud, ansible, black, pytest, rubocop, rspec, composer, artisan, eslint, npm:
hundreds of everyday command-line tools are written in Python, Ruby, PHP or Node, and spend
most of each call starting the interpreter and loading their code before doing any work.
speedrunner does that once, in a daemon, and forks it for every call: often 3 to 10 times
faster, with no per-tool setup.

- **A checks script.** The bash script below, built for this demo and replayable
 (bench/demo), runs a small shop's checks: black, pytest, poetry, rubocop, rspec,
 phpunit, artisan, aws and ansible, dozens of calls doing real work. 24.0 s natively, 5.3 s with
 `speedrunner exec`, its daemons warm: x4.5, same output (2-vCPU VPS). On a first run, its daemons
 stopped, about x3 (runs).
- **An editor's save.** eslint on one file: 328 → 43 ms; mypy: 213 → 50 ms. Faster than the tools'
 own daemons, eslint_d and dmypy (below).
- **A commit.** pre-commit with black, isort, flake8 and mypy on a changed file: 1.11 → 0.31 s with
 `speedrunner exec git commit`, same output (hooks declared `language: system`;
 details).
- **Never run twice.** Until a call has started, any problem sends it to the real tool, natively.
 Once it has started, speedrunner never runs it again, whatever dies.
- **Same output.** Identical to the native run on all 96 commands measured below; what speedrunner
 cannot serve faithfully runs natively.

speedrunner demo: the same bash script, run natively and with speedrunner

```bash
srr aws s3 ls                      # any Python, Ruby, PHP or Node tool, nothing to set up
speedrunner exec ./script.sh       # a whole script: every tool it calls, preloaded
eval "$(speedrunner activate)"     # at the top of a script: no prefix needed after
eval "$(speedrunner init zsh)"     # in ~/.zshrc (or init bash, in ~/.bashrc): daemons warm up while you type
speedrunner enroll aws             # then plain `aws s3 ls` in zsh or bash
```

Every command and option, why a call runs natively, where files live, and how to
uninstall: the user guide.

## Install

Linux (x86_64 or aarch64, any distribution) and macOS 11 or later (Intel or Apple Silicon): one binary, no root.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anthonyGosme/speedrunner/main/install.sh | sh
```

It checks the download's SHA-256 sum and installs `speedrunner` and its `srr`
link where your shell finds them: `/usr/local/bin` as root, otherwise
`~/.local/bin` (added to your PATH in `~/.profile`, `~/.bashrc` and `~/.zshrc`
if it is not there yet; `SPEEDRUNNER_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1` to leave them alone). Rather not pipe to `sh`? Take the archive and its
`.sha256` from the releases.
Or with a package manager. Homebrew, on macOS and Linux:

```bash
brew install anthonyGosme/speedrunner/speedrunner
```

Debian and Ubuntu (amd64, arm64), from the signed APT repository, so that
`apt upgrade` brings each release:

```bash
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSLo /etc/apt/keyrings/speedrunner.asc https://anthonygosme.github.io/speedrunner/apt/speedrunner.asc
sudo curl -fsSLo /etc/apt/sources.list.d/speedrunner.sources https://anthonygosme.github.io/speedrunner/apt/speedrunner.sources
sudo apt update && sudo apt install speedrunner
```

The `.sources` entry trusts that key for this repository only. Or, without
updates, the `.deb` of a release: `sudo apt install ./speedrunner_ _amd64.deb`.

On Arch Linux, `makepkg -si` in packaging/aur builds and installs the
package; it will be on the AUR as `speedrunner-bin` once registration reopens.

After v0.3.0, each archive and .deb also comes with a signed build provenance:
`gh attestation verify --repo anthonyGosme/speedrunner` checks that this
repository's release workflow built it from the tagged commit.
Each tool's daemon runs on that tool's own interpreter: nothing else to install
(PHP tools need PHP's FFI extension, and Node tools Node 22.15 or later for the daemon to learn what
they load; otherwise they gain less, or simply run natively).

Tested, with the whole regression suite, on Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04,
Alpine 3.20 and Fedora 42, with Python 3.9 to 3.14, Ruby 3.0 to 3.4, PHP 8.1
to 8.5 and Node 22 and 24, as root and as an unprivileged user (`docker/test-all.sh`); and on
macOS 15 (Intel) and macOS 26 (Apple Silicon), on every release.

Then see what it gains on your machine, with the tools you have:

```bash
speedrunner demo
```

## Results

 
**96 commands served (46 Python, 18 Ruby, 19 PHP, 13 Node), 96 with an output identical to the native run. Speedup: geometric mean x5.6, median x4.9; 77 at x3 or more, 21 at x10 or more.**

69 of them only print a version or a help text, which measures start-up alone. The 27 that do real work (lint or format a file, run tests, list a project) gain x4.0 median, 22 of them x3 or more.

Measured on a 2-vCPU Debian 12 VPS, or, for the commands marked ¹, on a laptop (Intel i7-9750H), in a Debian 12 container (Python 3.11.2, Ruby 3.1.2, PHP 8.2.35, Node 24.22.2). Warm daemon, no tool-specific setup: each command is simply run as `srr `. Each time is the median of 20 runs, native and speedrunner interleaved; the speedup is the ratio of the medians, with its 95% confidence interval (bootstrap). Every output (exit code, stdout, stderr) is compared with the native run's. Mean, standard deviation, min, max, the daemons' memory and every run: 20261030T212139Z-panel-vps; 20261030T210248Z-candidates-docker; 20261031T005026Z-node-panel-docker.

**Python**

| Command | Native | speedrunner | Speedup (95% CI) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `dbt --help` ¹ | 2721 ms | 30 ms | **x90.5** (83.8–93.2) |
| `copier --version` ¹ | 592 ms | 17 ms | **x34.7** (33.6–35.7) |
| `mycli --version` ¹ | 538 ms | 19 ms | **x28.4** (27.9–28.8) |
| `openstack --version` ¹ | 1055 ms | 42 ms | **x24.9** (23.8–26.6) |
| `airflow version` ¹ | 2254 ms | 98 ms | **x23.1** (22.8–23.4) |
| `pgcli --version` ¹ | 428 ms | 19 ms | **x22.2** (21.8–23.3) |
| `poetry --version` | 287 ms | 13 ms | **x21.7** (20.9–22.8) |
| `cookiecutter --version` ¹ | 386 ms | 20 ms | **x18.9** (16.4–22.6) |
| `litecli --version` ¹ | 307 ms | 18 ms | **x17.4** (17.3–17.7) |
| `pipenv --version` ¹ | 537 ms | 33 ms | **x16.4** (16.1–16.8) |
| `ansible --version` | 213 ms | 13 ms | **x15.9** (15.4–16.3) |

### Against the tools' own daemons

Some tools ship a daemon of their own because they start too slowly. The case
they were made for, an editor saving a file (one small file, changed before
every call so that no result cache answers), 20 interleaved runs in a Debian 12
container on a laptop:

| Tool | Native | speedrunner | Its own daemon |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| eslint | 328 ms | **43 ms** (x7.6) | 107 ms, `eslint_d` (x3.1) |
| prettier | 211 ms | **62 ms** (x3.4) | 105 ms, `prettierd` (x2.0) |
| rubocop | 297 ms | **108 ms** (x2.8) | 303 ms, `rubocop --server` (x1.0) |
| mypy | 213 ms | **50 ms** (x4.2) | 147 ms, `dmypy` (x1.4) |
| black | 241 ms | 26 ms (x9.4) | **19 ms**, `blackd` + `curl` (x12.7) |

A dedicated daemon's client is itself a Node, Python or Ruby process that
starts on every call; speedrunner's is a Rust binary that starts in about a
millisecond, and the tool runs in an already loaded fork. blackd wins with
`curl` as its client. On a large project, a dedicated daemon keeps state that
speedrunner rebuilds on every call (dmypy's incremental state, typescript-eslint's
program) and may come out ahead; this panel does not measure that.
Protocol and analysis.

## FAQ

**How much memory?** One daemon per tool, while you use it: 28 to 40 MB for a typical Python, Ruby or
PHP tool (median PSS, shared pages split fairly), about 60 MB for a Node tool, up to 200 MB for the
largest. Eleven tools at once: 341 MB. A daemon exits after 4 hours unused
(`SPEEDRUNNER_IDLE_TIMEOUT`, in seconds), or at once with `speedrunner stop `.

**And the first call?** It runs natively while the tool's daemon starts beside it (a little slower than
native: 15 to 40 ms for aws); the gain starts with the second call. In zsh or bash, `speedrunner init zsh` (or `bash`)
starts the daemon as you type the tool's name, so that even the first call is fast. In a script,
`speedrunner exec` starts, before they are reached, the daemons of the tools it will call more than once.

**When does it not help?** When the command's own work or the network dominates (`phpstan analyse`,
`aws s3 ls` on a slow link), for tools that start threads as they load (vite), and for native binaries:
there is nothing to preload.

**pre-commit, git hooks?** Commit with `speedrunner exec git commit`. git runs pre-commit's hook by its
path, but the hook's `#!/usr/bin/env bash` looks bash up on PATH: next to pre-commit's link, `exec` puts a
`bash` link that recognises pre-commit's hook and serves pre-commit itself; any other bash call goes
straight to the real bash. pre-commit's default hooks run from environments of its own, by absolute path,
so they stay native. Declare them `language: system` and they are served too: black, isort, flake8 and
mypy on a changed file, 1.11 s → 0.31 s per commit, same output
(details, in French).

**Node?** Supported since 0.3, as experimental. To fork V8, the daemon runs Node single-threaded
(`--single-threaded`), which can slow down tools that compute a lot; and it needs Node 22.15 or later to
learn what a tool loads.

**macOS, Windows?** macOS 11 or later, Intel and Apple Silicon, since 0.4.0: one universal
binary, which `install.sh` picks. Python, Ruby, PHP and Node are served, launchers (az, gcloud) followed; the bash
hook needs bash 4.2 or later (zsh, the default shell, has no such limit). Linux: x86_64 or aarch64, any
distribution. Windows: not planned.

Using it day to day: the user guide.

How it works, and the pitfalls met on the way: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

comments.author: anthonygosme
comments.text:
Hi HN, I'm Anthony.So I was getting tired of waiting around for all my command-line tools to start up. And sure, you might say, a few hundred milliseconds isn't that much. But multiply that by dozens and dozens of calls from ci/cd and scripts, and now you're starting to talk about a real slowdown.And then I thought, well, maybe I'll just write my own OS. But then I actually looked at the numbers, and most of that time isn't spent in the kernel. It's spent starting up the interpreter and loading the code for my tools.And then it hit me. What if I just loaded each of my tools once, kept them in memory, and then forked a copy whenever I actually needed one? And maybe I'd even write the client in Rust so it would be blazing fast.So how much of an improvement is there? Well, I've got a benchmark in the repo that runs eslint on a file. Natively it takes 328 ms, and with a warm daemon it takes 43 ms, so that's pretty sweet.And of course there's a whole bunch of commands, 96 in all, and 69 of them just print out a version or a help page or something like that. The median speedup is actually 4.9x, but if I just look at the 27 commands that actually do something, then it's more like 4x. And all 96 gave the same output and exit code as running them normally.One thing I really wanted to avoid was running a command twice. So if something goes wrong before it starts, speedrunner falls back to the normal tool. But once it's started, it won't run it again.And of course the first call still runs natively if the daemon isn't already up and running, and there's some memory usage. But the idea isn't entirely new. Spring does this sort of thing for Rails, there's Nailgun for the JVM, and JumpTheGun and quicken do something similar for Python. But this is an attempt to generalize it across multiple languages. And Node is still a little bit experimental. It runs on Linux and macOS, but not Windows.To try it, install speedrunner and run: speedrunner demo

It measures the gains using whichever tools it recognizes on your machine. So if you don't have many of those installed, there won't be as much to measure. And I'd be happy to hear which tools it doesn't serve very well, or what fork pitfalls I've missed.

title: Show HN: Ramen Profitable, a browser game about bootstrapping a SaaS
author: pierquinto
body:
Ramen Profitable 
 Your runs Leaderboard Updates Settings Sponsor Sign in Play now 
 Open menu 
Free browser game about indie hacking
 52 weeks to take a SaaS from idea to €10,000 MRR
 You quit your job with €12,000 in savings and €1,500 a month in expenses. Every week you pick one move. The market, your users, your cat and your mother take care of the rest.
 Play free Share a past run See the leaderboard 
 No download, no account needed. Sign in with an email link to save your endings.
 weeks to make it 52 weeks to make it 
 moves, one per week 6 moves, one per week 
 starting ideas, plus yours 9+1 starting ideas, plus yours 
 endings to discover 7 endings to discover 
 How a run works
 One move per week. Each one costs energy, and energy is the only thing you can't buy.
 Build
 Push the product forward. At 20% it goes live. Every week of code is worth a little less than the last.
Build in public
 Post about what you're making. Followers today, signups once the product is live.
Talk to users
 Calls with real people. More conversions, less churn and a list of tiny missing features.
Launch
 A spike of signups. Once every six weeks, and each launch works a bit less than the one before.
Freelance
 €1,400 in the bank and a week not spent on your product. Sometimes it's the right call.
Unplug
 A week offline to get your energy back. Below 30 every move yields less. At zero it's burnout.
Two finish lines
 €1,500 MRR
 Ramen profitable
 Enough for rent and ramen. The first milestone that keeps you out of an office.
€10,000 MRR
 Freedom
 At week 52, not before. Getting there early doesn't end the run: you can still burn out or slip back.
Things happen
 A VC offers you money. A funded competitor shows up. Product Hunt, viral threads, churn waves, acquisition offers, and your mother calling to ask how it's going. Every week brings an event, and every answer has a cost.
Seven endings
 From the exit to burnout, with a few surprises in between. The ones you haven't seen stay a mystery until you get there.
Pick an idea, or bring your own
 Each run deals three starting ideas from a deck of nine, from invoicing for freelancers to bookings for restaurants. Each one has its own price, audience, churn and world.
 Invoicr
 Streakd
 Shot2Code
 Tablr
 Swatchd
 Bouncd
 Repsy
 Inboxly
 Reportfox
 Or describe your own SaaS idea in a sentence. An AI estimates price, audience and churn from the real market, then the game balances it so it stays playable. Custom ideas need a free account.
Questions
 What is Ramen Profitable?
 + A free narrative game that runs in your browser. You play a solo founder who quits their job to build a SaaS, with 52 in-game weeks to reach €10,000 in monthly recurring revenue (MRR). It's made by Pierquinto Manco, an indie hacker from Milan.
 What does "ramen profitable" mean?
 + It's a term coined by Paul Graham in 2009: a startup that makes just enough money to pay the founders' living expenses, ramen included. In the game the threshold is €1,500 of MRR.
 Is it free? Do I need an account?
 + It's free and you can play as a guest. A free account, with a sign-in link sent by email and no password, saves your endings, puts you on the leaderboard and unlocks custom ideas.
 Can I play with my own startup idea?
 + Yes. Describe it in a sentence and the game turns it into a playable SaaS, with its own price, audience and churn. Custom ideas have their own leaderboard.
 How realistic is the simulation?
 + It's a game, not a financial model. But the mechanics come from real indie hacking: churn that eats your growth, launches with diminishing returns, conversions that improve when you talk to users, runway that runs out, and energy that runs out first.
 Does it work on mobile?
 + Yes, it runs in any modern browser, on desktop and on mobile. The room is drawn in 3D with WebGL, so an older phone may struggle a little.
 Which languages is it in?
 + English and Italian. You can switch from the game's title screen or from the settings.
Week 1 starts now
 The coffee is hot and the cat is already sitting on the keyboard.
 Play free

title: Show HN: 8 years of "Who's Hiring?" in charts (hiring boom, bust, and AI trends)
author: LanceJones
body: After seeing Andrej's HackerTube post (and given my sons are both junior-mid developers) I decided to point Codex at 8 years of "Who's hiring?" posts and rip through some tokens on semantic analysis of all that content. I started pre-COVID, thru October 2026, and the data was retrieved via HN API data.5 things that stand out:1. AI is now in half the posts. AI or machine learning appeared in 50% of 2026 posts, up from 17% in 2019.2. Most employers posted in only one month. Across all 94 monthly threads, 53% of the employers we identified appeared in just one month.3. Frontend roles fell from 16% to 3% of posts. That’s a substantial shift in the kinds of developers companies explicitly say they’re looking for.4. Staff-level posts grew 3.6×. Posts naming staff-level roles rose from 77 in 2019 to 277 in 2026, even as the hiring board got smaller.5. Only 41 posts explicitly named junior roles in 2026. Out of 2,932 posts. In 2019, there were 163.... plus 20 other trends.It feels like there's plenty to consider and discuss. Hope it's useful.

title: Show HN: Fooboard – deployment and promotion status of each repo per environment
author: karmaniverous
body:
fooboard
Welcome to DevOps hell. Here's your map.
fooboard: a deployment status board. To set up a board with an AI
 assistant, read
 https://www.fooboard.dev/ai .
fooboard shows the deployment state of every repo × stage at a
 glance: the status of each repo's latest deployment to each
 environment, and whether a stage's branch is behind, or has
 diverged from, the stage it is promoted from. It fills itself in
 from your GitHub Actions runs and, if you use them, AWS Amplify
 builds, with no workflow changes.
It is a free, open-source (BSD-3-Clause), static web app: no
 backend, no account, no cookies or telemetry. Your tokens and keys
 never leave your browser except in the calls it makes directly to
 GitHub and AWS.
An AI assistant can set up a board with you from the instructions at
 /ai: it asks about your repos and stages and gives you a link, and
 fooboard asks for your keys when you open it, so they never pass
 through the assistant.

# CVE Intel

 Know which vulnerabilities matter, and what to do about them. A private desktop app for vulnerability triage and scanning, written in native Rust, with a CLI, REST API and MCP server for developers and AI agents. 41 MCP tools, 41 data sources, SBOMs in and out, on-device AI. 

 

 

 Sped-up demo on macOS (1080p video): the threat landscape, triage and recording a decision, the decision ledger, a scan with attack chains and an SBOM, and the watchlist. 

## What is CVE Intel?

Every known software vulnerability gets a public ID, such as CVE-2024-3400. For each one, security, IT and development teams face the same question: does this affect us, and do we fix it now or can it wait? Answering it usually means checking NVD, CISA, FIRST, GitHub and vendor advisories by hand, one browser tab at a time.

### Why it matters now

CVE publication keeps rising (48,185 in 2025, 20.6% more than 2024, and over 86,000 by 27 October 2026), and in April 2026 NIST said the National Vulnerability Database cannot keep up, so it will enrich CVEs in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, federal-use software and critical software first, and move its unenriched backlog from before 1 March 2026 to "Not Scheduled". Meanwhile, Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 estimates the mean time to exploit at −7 days, so exploitation routinely begins before a patch is released, and exploits were the most common initial infection vector for the sixth year running (32% of intrusions).

### What it does

Give CVE Intel a CVE ID, a project folder, a lockfile or SBOM, a container image, the software on this computer, your own domains, or a suspicious IP address, file hash or domain. It queries up to 41 public sources, including CISA KEV, FIRST's EPSS and ENISA's EU Vulnerability Database alongside NVD, and returns what the vulnerability is, a risk score from 0 to 100, whether attackers are already using it, the evidence behind each signal and what to do next. It also shows what changed this week across those sources, and watches the vendors, products and packages you run.

- 41 data sources for vulnerability, exploit, network and threat intelligence, listed under Data sources. Many need no API key.
- 41 MCP tools for AI agents and coding assistants. The same program is also a command line and a REST API (see Developer notes).
- SBOMs in and out. It reads CycloneDX and SPDX SBOMs along with lockfiles, and Save SBOM (or `scan deps . --format cyclonedx`) writes any scan as a CycloneDX 1.5 SBOM with the findings, their risk signals and your recorded decisions.
- Local. There is no CVE Intel account or server. Lookups go straight from your computer to the public sources, and the AI assistant runs on a local model unless you choose a remote provider.

It is for security analysts, IT and operations teams, developers checking their dependencies, and anyone learning vulnerability management.

### What it helps you do

- Decide whether to patch now. Enter a CVE ID and get a risk score from 0 to 100, a plain recommendation and how urgent it is, with the evidence behind it.
- Put a list of vulnerabilities in order. Paste up to 10 CVE IDs from a scanner report and get the order to patch them in.
- Check your project's dependencies. Drop a project folder on the window, or paste a lockfile or SBOM. You see which packages have known vulnerabilities, ranked by how likely they are to hurt you (Log4Shell first, not just the highest CVSS), and which version fixes them. Scan again later to see what is new, fixed or riskier since last time, or save the scan as a CycloneDX SBOM with the findings in it.
- Check what you run and ship. Scan the apps and operating system on this computer, or a container image you build (no Docker needed). Or see what public sources already know about your own domains and servers, without CVE Intel ever connecting to them.
- See what affects the products you run. List the known vulnerabilities for a product and version, such as Apache Tomcat 9.0.80, with actively exploited ones first.
- See what changed this week. Open Landscape for new CISA KEV entries, CVEs ENISA marks exploited that KEV does not list yet, rising EPSS scores, new Metasploit modules and PoCs, new critical CVEs, Project Zero's in-the-wild zero-days and the latest CISA advisories. CVEs that several sources agree on are listed first.
- Watch the products you run. Add a vendor, product, package or CVE to the local watchlist. Each refresh records what changed: new CVEs, KEV listings, EPSS jumps, new exploits, CVSS revisions and newly available fixes.
- Remember what you decided, and hear when the reasons change. Record a decision on a CVE (patch now, defer until a date, accept the risk, not affected, mitigated) with the assumptions it rests on. Every refresh re-checks them: a deferral turns stale the day the CVE enters CISA KEV or an exploit appears, and the ledger tells you how your past calls held up.
- Keep an eye on what attackers are exploiting. Filter CISA's catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities by vendor, product, ransomware use or date.
- Investigate something suspicious. Check an IP address from your logs, a file hash your antivirus flagged, or an unfamiliar domain or URL against threat-intelligence sources.
- Ask questions in plain English."Should we patch CVE-2024-3400 this weekend?" The AI assistant looks up the facts first, then explains them, and shows which sources it used.
- Give AI coding assistants the same knowledge. Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and other tools can use CVE Intel while they work, through MCP.

### Terms you'll see

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| CVE | A public ID for one known vulnerability, such as CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell). |
| CVSS | A 0–10 severity score: how bad the flaw is if someone exploits it. It says nothing about how likely an attack is. |
| EPSS | The probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days, published daily by FIRST. |
| CISA KEV | The US government's catalog of vulnerabilities known to be exploited by attackers. A CVE on this list is urgent. |
| ENISA EUVD | The EU vulnerability database. Its own "exploited" flag is independent of CISA KEV and can raise the SSVC Exploitation input. |
| Exploit / PoC | Public code that demonstrates or carries out an attack. A Metasploit module means the attack is packaged and easy to use. |
| SSVC | A decision method from CISA and CERT/CC that ends in one of four actions: Act, Attend, Track* or Track. |
| SBOM / lockfile | A list of every package your software uses, with exact versions. |
| MCP | Model Context Protocol, the standard way AI assistants call outside tools. |

The risk score combines these signals: severity (CVSS), the chance of exploitation (EPSS), confirmed exploitation (CISA KEV) and public exploit code. Anything on CISA KEV is always CRITICAL. See Risk score for the formula.

> CVE Intel helps you decide what to patch. It does not probe, port-scan or attack anything, and it does not apply fixes. Scans read what is already on your machine (dependency files, the software installed on this computer, a container image you choose) and send only package and product names and versions to OSV.dev and NVD. The exposure check is passive: it asks public sources (Shodan, certificate transparency logs) what they already know about domains and addresses you own, and sends nothing to them. Results are only as current as the public sources.

## Getting started

You don't need an account or any API keys to start. Most people are looking at their first result within a couple of minutes:

1. Download the app for your operating system and open it. The Landscape view loads first: what changed this week across the public sources.
2. Open CVE Triage, type a CVE ID such as `CVE-2024-3400` and press Triage, or click one of the examples under the search box. Press Watch CVE (or Watch next to the vendor) to be told when it changes.
3. Drag a project folder onto the window to check its dependencies, or open Scan and choose This computer to check the software installed on this machine. Findings come back ranked by real-world risk, with the version that fixes each one.
4. Press `⌘K` (`Ctrl+K` on Windows and Linux) to open Quick Find. Paste anything there (a CVE, IP address, file hash, domain, URL or `package:ecosystem:version`) and CVE Intel picks the right lookup.
5. Optional: in Settings → Data source API keys, add free API keys for faster lookups and more exploit data. See API keys.
6. Optional: open Local Model and download a model to use Ask AI with answers that never leave your computer.
7. Optional: open MCP Server to connect your AI coding assistant.

The buttons at the bottom of the sidebar switch between the light and dark themes and make the text larger or smaller. The version you are running is shown below them.

Everything up to Developer notes is about the desktop app. To use CVE Intel from a terminal, a script, a CI pipeline or another program, go straight to that section.

### Threat landscape

What changed recently, from several independent sources at once: new CISA KEV entries (with ransomware flags and vendor counts), CVEs ENISA EUVD marks exploited that CISA KEV does not list, the largest EPSS rises, new or updated Metasploit modules and PoC-in-GitHub repositories, newly published critical NVD CVEs, Project Zero's in-the-wild zero-days and the latest CISA advisories. Each panel names its source and when it was fetched, and the ⓘ on each tile explains what it counts. Your watchlist comes first, then the CVEs that appear in two or more panels. Each watched item is a chip that opens it in the Watchlist. Copy the briefing as Markdown for a ticket or weekly note. Ask "What's new this week?" in Ask AI for the same briefing.

### Watchlist

Watch the vendors, products, packages and CVEs you run. Each refresh compares them with the last check and records what changed: new CVEs, KEV listings, ransomware use, EPSS jumps, new exploits or Metasploit modules, CVSS changes, newly available fixes and ENISA exploitation reports. The first check of an item records a silent baseline. The list lives only on this machine (`~/.cve-intel/watch.db`, owner-only). While the app is open it can refresh on a schedule (every 6 hours by default; change or turn it off in Settings). AI agents can read the watchlist over MCP but cannot change it.

### Decisions

Every tool says what is risky. None remembers what you decided, why, and whether the reasons still hold. Decisions does. Press Record decision on a triage result, a scan finding or a comparison, choose a verdict (patch now, defer until a date, accept the risk, not affected, mitigated) and tick the assumptions it rests on. The machine-checked ones are pre-ticked from today's evidence: not in CISA KEV, EPSS below a threshold, no public exploit, no Metasploit module, local access only, needs privileges, needs user interaction, no fix yet, not marked exploited by ENISA, no ransomware use, CVSS below a threshold, the sources agree, NVD has not analysed it yet. The manual ones (not internet-facing, behind a WAF, a compensating control, not reachable, the vendor says not affected, or your own words) carry a review date.

Recording a decision adds the CVE to the watchlist, and every refresh re-checks the assumptions. The day the CVE enters KEV, EPSS crosses the threshold, an exploit or a fix appears, or NVD publishes its analysis, the decision turns stale with the exact reason, an event lands in the watchlist feed, and the Landscape counts it under Decisions to revisit. A deferral past its date is expired; a manual assumption past its review date is review due. Re-decide replaces a decision and keeps the old one as history; Close records whether it was patched, accepted for good, won't be fixed, or other.

The ledger also tells you how your judgment held up: of the CVEs you held back in the last 30, 90 or 365 days, how many later entered KEV, gained an exploit or rose in EPSS, and how many days after the decision; of the patch-now calls, how many were confirmed by KEV, an exploit or a high EPSS at the time or since. Export the ledger as OpenVEX or CycloneDX VEX for scanners and SBOM consumers (the CycloneDX document lists each decided-on package as a component, so its references resolve in Dependency-Track and the like). It lives only on this machine (`~/.cve-intel/decisions.db`, owner-only); AI agents can read it over MCP (`list_decisions`, `get_decision_calibration`) but never change it, and Ask AI mentions your decision when you ask about a CVE you decided on. From the terminal: `cve-intel decide record CVE-2025-12345 --verdict defer --until 2026-12-31 --auto`, then `decide list`, `decide check`, `decide calibration` and `decide export`.

### CVE Triage

One lookup across NVD, CVE.org, EPSS, CISA KEV, ENISA EUVD and public exploit sources. The result includes the risk score, a plain recommendation and urgency, and the evidence behind it: CVSS (and where it came from), 30-day EPSS probability and its recent trend, KEV dates, ENISA's exploited flag, CIRCL sightings (deep triage), and the exploit evidence found in Metasploit, Exploit-DB, Nuclei, GitHub, PoC-in-GitHub and, with a VulnCheck token, VulnCheck KEV and XDB. When NVD has not scored a CVE yet, the CNA's or CISA's score from the CVE.org record is used. Deep triage also returns a CISA SSVC decision, using CISA's own published SSVC assessment (Vulnrichment) where one exists. ENISA EUVD or VulnCheck KEV can raise SSVC Exploitation to `active`; they do not change the risk score.

Who says what. Every triage result also lays the sources side by side: NVD's own score and analysis status, the CNA's score, CISA's ADP (Vulnrichment) score and SSVC assessment, EPSS, CISA KEV, ENISA EUVD, VulnCheck KEV and, in deep triage, Microsoft, Red Hat and Ubuntu (press Check vendors on a standard triage to add them). It names where they disagree: scores 2 or more points apart, a CVE that NVD has not analysed (common since NVD limited its analysis in 2026), a critical score that attackers have ignored for six months, exploitation reported by a source other than CISA KEV, a distribution that says its build is not affected or will not be fixed, and rejected or disputed CVEs. The card is marked Sources agree, Sources disagree or Thin evidence, and the same appears as the Agreement row in Compare CVEs, in the `consensus` field of `triage_cve`, and in the CLI's triage output. None of it changes the risk score.

Exploit speed. EPSS is a daily statistical model and the exploit indexes record what already exists; both lag. With language models reading patches, the public fix commit of an open-source CVE is itself a leading signal. A standard or deep triage therefore shows an Exploit speed estimate: Hours, Days, Weeks, Unknown, or Exploit exists when a PoC or a KEV listing already makes the question moot. It starts at 30 points and adds or subtracts for the fix (a small, localised public fix with a test that encodes the trigger counts most; no public fix at all counts against), the weakness class (injection, traversal, authentication bypass and deserialisation are fast; memory corruption and races are slow), the CVSS vector (network, no privileges, no user interaction) and the time already elapsed without a PoC. Every line of the rationale is shown, the label says estimate, the confidence never exceeds medium, and without a public fix the label is capped at Days. Fix commits come from the references NVD, CVE.org, OSV and GitHub Advisories tag as the patch and are read from GitHub (two requests per CVE at most; a free token raises the limit from 60 to 5,000 an hour). The same estimate is a row in Compare CVEs, a chip on the riskiest unexploited findings of a scan, the `exploit_speed` field of `triage_cve` and `scan_dependencies`, and the fix date on `get_cve_timeline`. It never changes the risk score.

The interface follows your system's light or dark theme until you pick one with the sun and moon button at the bottom of the sidebar. Beside it, A− and A+ make the text and controls smaller or larger in every view (`⌘ −`, `⌘ +` and `⌘ 0` on macOS; `Ctrl` on Windows and Linux), and the size is remembered.

### Ask in plain language

Ask questions such as "Which is worse: CVE-2024-3400 or CVE-2023-44487?" CVE Intel runs the lookups first, then the model explains the results and lists the tools it used. Small local models can still get details wrong, so check an answer you will act on against CVE Triage.

### Compare and prioritise

Paste 2 to 10 CVE IDs to compare them and get a patch order based on KEV status, score, EPSS and exploit evidence, not on CVSS alone. Not sure where to start? The examples under the box (KEV vs. CVSS, VPN & firewall zero-days, Microsoft patch day and Open-source libraries) each show one way the order can surprise you.

CISA KEV CVEs come first, then the risk score. Equal scores are common (exploited CVEs with a high EPSS all reach 100), so ties are broken by known ransomware use, EPSS, exploit maturity, CVSS and the earlier KEV due date. Each CVE says why it sits above the next one.

- Side by side: one column per CVE, with rows for the score's parts, KEV dates, ransomware use, who reports exploitation, EPSS and its 30-day trend, exploit sources, CVSS attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction and impact, product, CWE and age. Riskier values that differ are in red. Only rows that differ hides the rest.
- What they have in common: CVEs in the same product (one update may cover them) or from the same vendor, ransomware use, exploitation reported outside CISA KEV (which the score doesn't count), network access without sign-in or user action, public exploits, rising EPSS, and shared weaknesses.

### Scan dependencies

Drop a project folder or dependency files anywhere on the window, or use Choose folder… / Choose files…. A folder is searched, including subfolders, for the lockfiles, manifests and SBOMs listed below. The search skips `node_modules`, virtualenvs, `vendor`, build output and hidden folders, and skips a `package.json` or `go.sum` that sits next to the lockfile that pins it. Each file found is listed with its format and package count. Untick any you don't want, then press Scan. Every file is parsed on its own, a package listed in several files is checked once, and each finding names the files it came from. Files are read on your machine; only package names and versions are sent to OSV.dev.

You can also paste a lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`, `Pipfile.lock`, `poetry.lock`, `uv.lock`, `Cargo.lock`, `go.sum`, `go.mod`, `composer.lock`, `Gemfile.lock`), an SBOM (CycloneDX JSON or XML, SPDX JSON or tag-value), a `requirements.txt`, `package.json` or `pom.xml`, purls, or `name:ecosystem:version` lines (for example from `apk info -v` or `dpkg -l`; Alpine needs its release, as in `openssl:Alpine:v3.19:3.1.4-r0`). The format is detected automatically and up to 10,000 packages are checked against OSV.dev.

Findings are ranked by risk, not just severity. Each one gets the same signals as CVE Triage: whether its CVE is in CISA KEV (and used by ransomware), its EPSS score, exploit evidence from Exploit-DB and Metasploit, and the risk score. Log4Shell in an old `log4j-core` comes out on top; a CVSS 9.8 nobody exploits does not. When GitHub, PyPI and a distribution each publish the same issue, it is shown once. Filter by risk, KEV or whether a fix exists, or switch to By package to see each vulnerable package with its advisories and the version that fixes them. In a CI pipeline the same scan can fail the build or feed GitHub code scanning; see CI and automation.

Every scan is saved in History, on this computer only. Scan the same folder again (or press Scan again) and the results say what changed since the scan before: findings that are new, resolved (and whether an upgrade or a removal fixed them), or riskier because they were added to CISA KEV, gained an exploit or jumped in EPSS. A pasted list is saved under a hash of its packages, never its text. Copy as Markdown puts the findings table on the clipboard for a ticket, and Forget deletes every scan of a target.

Save SBOM writes the scan you just ran as a CycloneDX 1.5 document: every package or app it read, clean ones included, each finding as a vulnerability affecting its component with the risk signals (KEV, EPSS, exploit evidence, risk score) and the fix version, and your recorded decision on it as the `analysis`. It is a scan-derived inventory (what the lockfiles, image or this computer declared, with no supplier, hashes, licences or dependency graph), and says so in its metadata; a build-time generator such as Syft or cdxgen remains the authoritative source for those. Load it into Dependency-Track, attach it to a release, or hand it to an auditor. The same document comes from `cve-intel scan deps . --format cyclonedx` on the command line.

Chains. A ranked list hides chains: a LOW local privilege escalation and a HIGH network RCE on the same host are a full compromise together. The Chains tab of every scan links the findings of a target into attack chains, from network entry through code execution, privilege escalation, credential access or persistence to an outcome. Each step names its basis: the CVSS vector (network, no privileges, scope change), the weakness, CTID's curated KEV → ATT&CK mapping, or an inference from the weakness through CAPEC. Chains get a transparent score (stages covered, the riskiest step, an exploited entry, an unfixed privilege escalation) that never touches a finding's risk score, and the callout at the top names the break point: the finding whose fix cuts the most chains, which may well be that LOW. On this computer and in a container image a chain may start at code execution, since code already runs there. Every result states its assumptions: all findings of a target are treated as present together, and nothing is known about reachability or mitigations. The chains are in the scan's Markdown, in `scan … --chains` and `scans show … --chains` on the command line, and in the read-only `get_scan_chains` tool for local agents.

Watch all affected adds the affected packages and apps of a scan to the Watchlist, riskiest first, so you hear when one of them is added to CISA KEV or gains an exploit. Tick Monitor next to a target in History to have CVE Intel scan it again every day while the app is open (the same folders, this computer, the same image or the same exposure targets); what becomes new or riskier appears in the Watchlist feed and on the Landscape.

### Scan this computer

Scan → This computer checks the operating system and the apps installed on this machine. On Windows they come from the registry (the programs in Installed apps, including per-user installs) and the Windows build; on macOS from Applications, ~/Applications, Homebrew (Apple silicon and Intel) and the macOS version. List installed software shows what was found and what will be checked, without contacting anything. Check sends NVD only the vendor, product and version of the apps CVE Intel recognises (browsers, Java, Acrobat, archivers, remote-access tools, VPN clients, developer tools and about 100 more) and of the OS, then ranks the findings like any other scan.

On Linux the distribution's packages come from its package database (dpkg, apk, rpm or pacman) and are checked with OSV.dev. Arch Linux is the exception: OSV has no Arch packages, so they are checked against the Arch Linux Security Tracker instead. Its whole list is downloaded and matched on your machine with pacman's version order, so no package names are sent. Arch derivatives (Manjaro, EndeavourOS, CachyOS, Garuda, Artix, SteamOS) are matched against it too, with a note that packages they build themselves can differ from Arch's. The tracker leaves many advisories marked unfixed long after upstream fixed them, so an unfixed advisory confirmed only in an older upstream version than the one installed is listed as not checked, with the advisory, rather than reported as a finding. A rebuild of the confirmed version (a new pkgrel only) is still a finding. Packages from third-party repositories and the AUR that CVE Intel recognises (Chrome, Edge, Brave, VS Code) are checked with NVD.

Apps CVE Intel does not recognise are listed as not checked, with the reason. Tick Also look up apps CVE Intel does not recognise to ask NVD's product dictionary for them: this sends their names to NVD, and a match is kept only when NVD's vendor fits the app's publisher. Without an NVD API key NVD allows a few requests a minute, so a first scan checks the riskiest apps (browsers, Java, Acrobat, the OS) first and leaves the rest for the next scan; answers are cached, so later scans are quicker. Programs that are parts of others (system components, drivers) are skipped, and Microsoft 365 and the Visual C++ runtimes are reported as not checked because NVD lists them without versions.

### Scan a container image

Scan → Container image checks a saved image without Docker: drop a `docker save` or OCI archive (`.tar`, `.tar.gz`) on the window, or choose an OCI layout folder. The image is read on your computer in one pass, layer by layer, without unpacking anything to disk. Its operating system packages (Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine, Wolfi, Chainguard, Red Hat, Rocky, AlmaLinux, Azure Linux and openSUSE) and any lockfiles, manifests or SBOMs inside it are checked with OSV.dev and ranked like any other scan. Arch Linux images are checked against the Arch Linux Security Tracker, matched locally. A multi-platform image is scanned for this computer's architecture unless you name another platform. Images whose distribution OSV does not cover (Fedora, Amazon Linux, SUSE Linux Enterprise, Debian testing) and older rpm databases are listed as not checked rather than reported clean.

```
docker save myapp:latest -o myapp.tar
cve-intel scan image myapp.tar --fail-on kev
```

### Check your public exposure

Scan → Public exposure shows what public sources already know about domains and addresses you own. Enter domains or public IP addresses, confirm they are yours (or that you are authorised to assess them), and press Find addresses: CVE Intel collects host names from certificate transparency logs (crt.sh, keeping only names under your domain), resolves them, and lists the public addresses, dropping private and reserved ones. Untick any that are not yours, then press Check. For each address it asks Shodan (with a Shodan key) or the free Shodan InternetDB what services, software versions and CVEs have been seen there, then checks the versions with NVD and ranks the findings like any other scan.

The check is passive: CVE Intel never connects to the targets, and nothing is port-scanned. Addresses that belong to a CDN or hosting platform are flagged and left out, because the software seen there is the provider's. CVEs Shodan infers from a banner are marked as reported, not verified, and distribution builds (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL) may have the fix backported.

```
cve-intel scan exposure example.com --authorized --list-only   # names and addresses only
cve-intel scan exposure example.com 203.0.113.10 --authorized --max-ips 20
```

### Databases and data sources

See every upstream source: what it provides, whether it needs a key, whether your key is set, how long results are cached, and which tools use it. Press Check connectivity to probe all of them live. The view also shows the local cache, downloaded models and the model runtime.

### MCP server for AI agents

Give AI agents CVE Intel's 41 tools while they work. Start the server from the app, choose your agent, and copy setup steps with the correct address and executable path already filled in. Guides are included for Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Claude Desktop, Windsurf and any other MCP client.

- Two ways to connect. The agent can connect over HTTP to the server the app runs, or launch its own copy over stdio. The stdio option works even when the app is closed.
- Simple control. Start and stop the server, pick a port (8000 by default), and optionally start it whenever the app opens. The sidebar shows whether it is running.
- Local only. The server listens on `127.0.0.1` and refuses requests from web pages, so websites and other computers cannot use it.
- Uses your saved keys. Agents get the same data sources and API keys you configured in Settings.

To configure an agent by hand instead, see MCP server setup.

### Also included

- Quick Find (`⌘K` or `Ctrl+K`): paste a CVE, IP, hash, domain, URL or `package:ecosystem:version` and CVE Intel picks the right lookup.
- Fixed versions: the version to upgrade a package to so that every known vulnerability is fixed, re-checked against OSV. Quick Find `lodash:npm:4.17.15` to see it, or ask in Ask AI.
- Product and KEV search: every CVE affecting a product and version, exploited ones first, and filters over the CISA KEV catalog by vendor, product, ransomware use or date. Available in Ask AI, the CLI and MCP.
- MITRE ATT&CK mapping: curated CTID mappings for KEV-listed CVEs, plus techniques inferred from the CVE's weaknesses through CAPEC, labelled as inferred. Available to AI agents over MCP and through the REST API.
- IP, hash and domain intelligence from AbuseIPDB, GreyNoise, Shodan, VirusTotal, MalwareBazaar, crt.sh and more. Private and internal IPs are rejected before any lookup is made.
- Activity view: a searchable local history of your lookups, answers and the tool calls agents made, which you can pause or clear.
- Local Model view: install the runtime and download a model in one click.
- System view: health and version information.

## Common uses

| Situation | What to do in the app |
| --- | --- |
| What happened this week? | Open Landscape, or ask "What's new this week?" in Ask AI. |
| A new CVE is in the news. Do we drop everything? | Enter it in CVE Triage, or ask "Should we patch CVE-2024-3400 this weekend?" in Ask AI. |
| We run Fortinet (or another vendor). Tell me when something new hits it. | Add the vendor on Watchlist, or press Watch next to the vendor on a triage result. |
| We decided not to patch something yet. Tell me if that stops being safe. | Press Record decision on the triage result and tick the reasons. Decisions marks it stale the moment one of them breaks. |
| A scanner reported 40 findings. Which come first? | Paste the IDs into Compare CVEs, up to 10 at a time. |
| Checking dependencies before a release. | Drop the project folder on Scan, or paste the lockfile or SBOM. Press Watch all affected to follow them, or Monitor in History to have it scanned again daily. |
| Is anything installed on this laptop being exploited? | Scan → This computer, then Check. Findings in CISA KEV come first. |
| Is the image we ship affected by a new KEV entry? | `docker save` it and drop the `.tar` on Scan → Container image. |
| What does the internet see on our servers? | Scan → Public exposure with your domain; passive, nothing connects to your hosts. |
| Which version of a library fixes everything? | Open Quick Find and paste `lodash:npm:4.17.15`. |
| What is known about the Tomcat version we run? | Ask "Which CVEs affect Apache Tomcat 9.0.80?" in Ask AI.¹ |
| Is anything from a vendor being exploited right now? | Ask "Which Fortinet vulnerabilities are in CISA KEV?" in Ask AI.¹ |
| An unknown IP appears in firewall or login logs. | Paste it into Quick Find. |
| EDR flags an unknown file. | Paste its SHA-256 hash into Quick Find. |
| You work in an AI coding tool. | Open MCP Server, start the server and copy the setup steps for your agent. |
| You are new to vulnerability management. | Ask "Explain EPSS and CISA KEV like I'm new." |

¹ For these questions the model has to pick the right lookup itself, which larger local models and cloud providers do more reliably. The same searches are always available from the terminal (see Recipes).

## Install

Download the file for your OS from the latest release. The desktop app, CLI, MCP server and REST API are all one executable, with nothing else to install.

| OS | File | How to run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Windows | `CVE-Intel_ _windows-x64-setup.exe` (or `…-portable.exe`) | Run the installer, then open CVE Intel |
| macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) | `CVE-Intel_ _macos-universal.dmg` | Drag CVE Intel to Applications |
| Linux | `CVE-Intel_ _linux-x64.AppImage` (or `.deb`) | `chmod +x` the file and run it |

Each file has a `.sha256` checksum next to it. Builds are not code-signed yet, so Windows SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper warn on first launch. On macOS, right-click the app and choose Open.

To build it yourself, run the headless server in Docker, or run the desktop app in a container and use it from your browser (no install), see Build from source and Docker.

## Local AI

Ask AI uses a small language model that runs on your computer, so your questions stay private. Before the model runs, CVE Intel finds the CVE IDs, IPs, hashes and domains in your question, runs the matching lookups and gives the model the results as facts to rely on. If no model is running, Ask returns those lookup results directly, so it is useful before any download finishes.

Open the Local Model view to install the llama.cpp runtime and download a model, one click each (files go under `~/.cve-intel/`). The default is Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct, a ~1.9 GB download that needs 6 GB of RAM; the 1B and 1.5B models need 4 GB and Qwen 2.5 7B needs 10 GB. On Apple silicon the view also offers two MLX models that run on the GPU and answer faster. The model server listens on `127.0.0.1` only. Already running Ollama, LM Studio or your own llama-server? See Use your own model server.

### Remote providers (opt-in)

For stronger answers, open Configure → Remote AI and choose OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint: a LiteLLM proxy, vLLM, Azure OpenAI, OpenRouter, Together, Groq, Ollama behind HTTPS… Paste a key (and for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, its base URL), then pick a model. Save & use enables the provider and tests it; Save without switching keeps your current choice. You can switch back to the local model at any time.

| Provider | Default model | Environment variables |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI | `gpt-4o` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| Anthropic | `claude-opus-5` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
| Google Gemini | `gemini-2.5-flash` | `GEMINI_API_KEY` |
| OpenAI-compatible endpoint (LiteLLM, vLLM, …) | (the server's model name) | `CUSTOM_LLM_BASE_URL`, `CUSTOM_LLM_API_KEY` (optional) |

Models come from the provider itself: once a key is saved, the model list is fetched live from the provider's `/models` endpoint, so it shows every model your key can use (for OpenAI and Gemini, embedding, speech and image models are left out). Press ↻ to refresh it, or choose Other to type any model ID. Until a key is saved, a few suggestions are shown. The same settings work from a terminal:

```
cve-intel ai list                                   # every provider, where it sends requests, what it still needs
cve-intel ai set anthropic --key                    # hidden prompt
cve-intel ai models anthropic                       # every model the key can use, fetched live
cve-intel ai set anthropic --model claude-opus-5 --use
cve-intel ai set custom --url https://litellm.example.com/v1 --key --model claude-sonnet-5 --use   # LiteLLM, vLLM, …
cve-intel ai test                                   # one tiny request to the provider in use
cve-intel ai use local                              # back to the on-device model
```

`--key` reads the key from a hidden prompt (or stdin when piped), never from the command line.

- Off by default. When a remote provider is selected, each question and the lookup results gathered for it are sent to that endpoint under its operator's terms. The Ask view shows a banner while this is on.
- Where requests go. OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini use built-in HTTPS addresses. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint must be `https://`; plain `http://` is accepted only to this machine (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`). A saved key is tied to its URL: changing the URL forgets the key, so it is never sent to a new host without being entered again. A key saved while the URL comes from `CUSTOM_LLM_BASE_URL` is saved with that URL, and `CUSTOM_LLM_API_KEY` is only sent to `CUSTOM_LLM_BASE_URL`. Requests to a loopback address skip `HTTPS_PROXY`.
- Keys stay local. Keys are stored in `~/.cve-intel/settings.db` with owner-only permissions. They are never shown again in the UI and never logged. You can use environment variables instead. See SECURITY.md.
- No vendor SDK. Every provider here offers an OpenAI-compatible chat API with tool calling. Anthropic describes its compatible endpoint as intended mainly for evaluation; for Claude-specific features, use CVE Intel through MCP in a Claude client.

title: Show HN: Open-source silent speech with $20 EMG sensors and a webcam
author: gottaguo
body:
# thaimtl/Silent-Voice

Silent speech for people who lost their voice box. Cal Hacks 13.0.

- Stars: 8
- Forks: 2
- Watchers: 8
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-24T01:16:57Z

## Languages

- Batchfile
- C++
- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Python
- Shell

## Top Contributors

- thaimtl (73 contributions)
- AustinKol (50 contributions)
- evanliuuu (11 contributions)
- FrankWoah (6 contributions)

---

## README

# Silent Voice

Silent Voice gives a voice back to people who lost their voice box.
You mouth the words without a sound, and Silent Voice speaks them in your own voice while you're still mouthing, even on a phone call.

We built it at Cal Hacks 13.0, where it placed 2nd overall and won Cartesia's voice AI challenge.
The story of the weekend is in Thai's writeup.

## Who it's for

A laryngectomy removes the voice box, usually after throat cancer.
People keep their lips, tongue, and jaw, so the words are still there, only the sound is gone.
Many of them speak through an electrolarynx, a handheld buzzer that sounds robotic and ties up a hand.
We think they deserve a voice that sounds like them, keeps up with a real conversation, and works on an ordinary phone call, and that's what we're building.

Our demo speaker is Austin, who's healthy, and no patients take part in the demo.

## How it works

Silent Voice has one mode, open mouth, no sound, in real time.
Three readers work together, because each one sees what the others can't.
Every 100 ms one joint search combines them and locks in each word as soon as they're confident enough.

 
 
 
 

- The camera reads the lips and does most of the work.
 It also reads the facial expression, which sets the voice's emotion.
- The EMG model reads the electrical signals of the face muscles, so it sees the tongue and jaw that no camera can.
 It settles words that look alike on the lips ("bat", "mat", "pat"), proposes its own guesses, and keeps going when the face is hard to see.
- Claude follows the whole conversation, both sides.
 It predicts likely words before you start mouthing and repairs look-alike mistakes ("bills" → "pills" after a question about medicine).
 It only swaps look-alike words and never adds ideas.
- Cartesia speaks each word in your cloned voice as soon as it locks, without waiting for the end of the sentence.
- When the system can't tell what you said, it shows "Please repeat" instead of guessing.

Read on for the details.

- docs/REALTIME_PIPELINE.md explains how the whole system works.
- docs/SVR1_SPEC.md specifies the EMG model, SVR-1.
- docs/TEAM_TASKS_AND_INTERFACES.md covers who builds what.
- HARDWARE.md describes the rig, and RECORDING.md the recording sessions.
- DEMO.md runs the demo: one launcher starts everything in order (`Launch Silent Voice.bat`).

## What we demo

The demo is two minutes, live, at our table.

1. Austin calls the judge standing in front of us, through Twilio.
 The judge talks normally, and their words appear in the captions.
2. Austin mouths his side of the conversation.
 His words appear as he mouths and play into the call in his cloned voice while he's still going.
3. His facial expression sets the voice's emotion.
4. The dashboard shows the real latency, which reader settled each word, and what Claude changed.

## Stack

| Part | Tool |
|---|---|
| Live lip reading | Ours (`lipread/`), built on the open Auto-AVSR model. We turned a clip-by-clip reader into a live one that streams word guesses as Austin mouths, knows when he starts and stops, and feeds every guess into one joint search with the EMG model and Claude. |
| Face, mouth crop, expression | MediaPipe FaceLandmarker |
| Muscle signals | BioAmp EXG Pill boards and an Arduino Uno, see HARDWARE.md |
| EMG model | SVR-1, ours: PyTorch, pre-trained on Berkeley's silent speech data, fine-tuned on Austin |
| Context and repairs | Claude, through the Claude API |
| Voice clone and speech | Cartesia Sonic 3.6, Instant Voice Clone |
| The other person's speech to text | Cartesia Ink |
| Phone call | Twilio |
| Compute | One laptop, RTX 5060 |

## Code and data

All code lives in this repo.
Datasets, checkpoints, results, and Python environments live in a working directory outside it, and the code finds them through the environment variable `RECLAIM_WORKDIR` (datasets in `silent_speech/` and `data/`, plus `checkpoints/`, `benchmark_results/`, `recordings/`, `third_party/`).
Without it, the code expects data next to itself, which is how the cluster copy works.
Data folders are in `.gitignore`.

| Folder | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `svr/` | SVR-1, the EMG model: model, training, fine-tuning, preprocessing (docs/SVR1_SPEC.md) |
| `fusion/` | The fusion process: the joint search over camera + EMG + Claude (`search.py`), the lock model (`lock.py`), on the bus (`run.py`), offline fitting and tests on the recordings (`offline.py`), and its language model: a conversational 4-gram with a cache of the call (`lm.py`, built by `build_lm.py`) |
| `bench/` | Benchmarks and their frozen test splits |
| `cluster/` | H100/H200 job scripts (PBS), smoke tests, runbook |
| `camera/` | Camera-only baselines (Auto-AVSR, BRAVEn, LipLearner) |
| `rig/` | EMG rig: Arduino firmware, serial reader, live hum filter, signal check, `emg.raw` publisher (`publish.py`) |
| `recorder/` | The recording app: camera + EMG + the session sentences (recorder/README.md) |
| `bus/` | The team bus: ZeroMQ wire format, the camera's topics (`__init__.py`) and every other endpoint and port (`team.py`); a fake camera (`stub.py`) and a typed stand-in for the judge (`type_judge.py`) for tests |
| `buslog/` | Logs every bus message to `$RECLAIM_WORKDIR/logs/` (`record.py`) and replays a session (`replay.py`) |
| `claude_service/` | The Claude service: predicts Austin's next words and repairs look-alikes (`brain.py`), on the bus (`service.py`) |
| `dashboard/` | The live dashboard judges watch, from Thai's Figma v5, fed by the bus (dashboard/README.md) |
| `demo/` | The demo launcher (`launch.py`, DEMO.md); `demo/dashboard/`: the captions dashboard prototype (demo/dashboard/README.md) |
| `call/` | The phone call: Twilio, Austin's cloned voice (Cartesia Sonic) and the judge's captions (Cartesia Ink) (call/README.md) |
| `figures/` | The SVR-1 architecture figure, the SVR-1 vs Gaddy & Klein results (`svr1_vs_gaddy_4ch*`), and the scripts that draw them |
| `tests/` | Smoke and unit tests |
| `docs/` | Plans and specs, Markdown with PDF copies |

## Known limitations

- This is a prototype, not a medical device.
- Lip reading gets about 1 in 5 words wrong even on normal speaking video, and silent mouthing is harder.
 The EMG model and Claude are there to close that gap.
- The EMG model is trained for one person (Austin), from three recording sessions, see RECORDING.md.
- The voice runs a little behind the lips, because a word is spoken only once it's confident enough to lock.

## Built on

- Digital Voicing of Silent Speech, Gaddy and Klein, UC Berkeley, 2020, for the electrode sites and pre-training data.
- Auto-AVSR, Ma et al., 2023, for lip reading.
- Lipflow, MIT license, for live mouth cropping with MediaPipe.

## Team

Thai (EMG hardware and the Claude service), Austin (EMG model and fusion, and the speaker in the demo), Frank (Cartesia voice, the Twilio call, and the captions dashboard), and Evan (real-time lip reading and facial emotion).

## License

Silent Voice is open source under the MIT license.
Bundled third-party files keep their own licenses, which are Mermaid (MIT, `docs/vendor/mermaid.LICENSE`), the Liberation Sans and Atkinson Hyperlegible Next fonts (SIL Open Font License 1.1), and MediaPipe's face mesh data (Apache-2.0).

comments.author: gottaguo
comments.text: Hi HN, Frank here. We placed second overall at Cal Hacks 13.0 (700+ projects), four of us from McGill.Over 200,000 people are diagnosed with throat cancer each year, and for many, the surgery removes their voice box. More than half a million people are already living without one.Their lips, tongue and jaw still move in the same way, but with nothing there to create any sound, they lose the ability to speak forever.In 36 hours we built Silent Voice to give them their voice back.With four different AI systems working together, Austin held a full phone call without making a sound, and the caller heard him in his own voice.• Muscles: we built a sensor rig using four surface EMG pads ($20 each) to measure the electrical activity in his face 1,000 times a second, and used a neural network (SVR-1) we'd trained to infer the movement of his tongue and jaw (which a camera can't see)• Lips: Auto-AVSR is a lip-reading technique which only works on complete video. We rebuilt it to work in real-time, re-reading Austin's sentence 10 times a second• Face: computer vision tracks his expressions and carries his emotion through the voice• Context: Claude uses both sides of the conversation to predict what Austin may say, and compensates for common confusions such as 'bills' and 'pills'SVR-1 is ~45M params, 12 transformer layers on top of 3 conv blocks, pretrained on Berkeley's 19h silent speech set then fine tuned on ~70 min of Austin. With only our 4 pads it picks the right sentence out of 10 lip look-alikes 72.3% of the time, Berkeley's released model gets 27.7% (theirs was trained on 8 pads though).I led the voice pipeline. Standard techniques rely on complete input, but we were only receiving individual words as Austin formed them. Waiting for a complete sentence meant callers were subjected to 4.9 seconds of dead air, whilst sending single words sounded like a robot reading a list.So I re-engineered the entire streaming layer into Cartesia, delivering complete (though brief) phrases in step with Austin's natural pauses, and cut the silence added by the model after each phrase (around half a second) down to a more natural (i.e. human) breath. His expression can also shift the emotion mid-sentence.As a result, callers were hearing Austin 0.6 seconds after his lips began to move, in real-time.It's a prototype, Austin is healthy and no patients have tried it yet. Code is open source, the demo is on the Devpost: https://devpost.com/software/silent-voice-s1f74pIf you've had (or know someone who's had) a laryngectomy, or work with them as a speech therapist, I'd love to hear from you.
